articles.title_orig: Pennsylvania faces largest measles outbreak in decades as case count rises to 1,000
articles.title_zh: Pennsylvania faces largest measles outbreak in decades as case count rises to 1,000
articles.content_orig:
Neighboring states are also reporting hundreds of cases, with over 3,800 recorded across the country
Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, state health officials calculate, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades. The benchmark comes as neighboring New York declared a state of emergency about measles rates there.
Pennsylvania’s health department said Monday 1,004 cases of measles had been confirmed. Five Pennsylvania residents ⁠have died ⁠after ​contracting the disease, with 198 hospitalizations.
Lancaster county, with sizeable Amish and Mennonite populations, remains the hardest hit, with 391 cases, according to official figures. Cases numbers have risen over the past three months, with the highest number of infections in the 24-49 age range.
The numbers, however, are not included in a CDC count due to an ongoing dispute between Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, and the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr over how to classify measles-related mortality.
Shapiro has called Kennedy “incompetent”, and Kennedy has publicly questioned whether the state’s recorded fatalities were directly caused by measles. The CDC – which Kennedy oversees – currently lists two measles deaths in the US this year.
Shapiro has expanded access to the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine in affected communities.
“I want every Pennsylvanian to know this: measles does not care about your county, your faith, or your social circle,” he said in August. “I urge everyone to take this seriously and to discuss any concerns with their trusted health care provider.”
In New York state, governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency on Monday as well, citing 108 cases in the state as of 3 October.
Ohio, which also shares a border with Pennsylvania, has also reported advancing numbers of cases, with more than 200 this year. Like in Pennsylvania, Ohio has a significant Amish population.
The US is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991. As of 1 October, the CDC reported 3,887 confirmed cases this year, along with the highest number of measles-associated deaths in decades.
In addition to Pennsylvania, outbreaks have been reported in several states, including Texas and Utah, as well as South Carolina, which had the largest outbreak with 997 cases reported.
Health officials in Pennsylvania have said the state’s current outbreak started in April, west of Philadelphia and attributed the outbreak to low vaccination rates.
According to the Associated Press, the most recent outbreak to surpass 1,000 cases occurred in New York City in the early 1990s . That outbreak infected more than 4,500 people. During the 1989 and 1991 resurgences, 55,000 infections and 123 deaths ⁠were recorded, according to Reuters.
The domestic US spread of measles was eliminated in 2000 by high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the US and Mexico have lost their measles-free status .

articles.title_zh: British Airways reveals all-new First, Club Suite, World Traveller Plus and World Traveller cabins as part of its multi-billion investment into customer experience
articles.content_orig:
Published: 13:25 EDT, 5 October 2026 | Updated: 21:31 EDT, 5 October 2026
A British Airways steward who was sacked for asking a female colleague if she wanted to join the 'mile-high club' has won almost £30,000 for unfair dismissal.
Charly Mateo, then aged 37, was sacked by the airline in July 2024 after 'disturbing' the cabin crew member on a flight months earlier.
An investigation by the airline found that Mr Mateo had 'purposely touched' his colleague's leg while she was on a mid-flight break behind a privacy curtain.
The steward, who was based out of Heathrow Airport, was also alleged to have told her 'sexual stories' about two other women.
He was later fired before suing the airline for unfair and wrongful dismissal, with an employment tribunal this week finding that BA did not conduct a thorough enough investigation into the allegations.
At Reading Employment Tribunal, Mr Mateo was awarded £29,195 despite it being heard that he acted in 'strange behaviour' and 'invaded her privacy'. His bid to be reinstated was, however, lost.
The tribunal heard: '[A colleague] reported that when the complainant had finished her break she had looked tired and had said about the conversation with [Mr Mateo], "I was just trying to be nice, but I need to learn how to be blunt with people" and further that the complainant had said she had not wanted to have a conversation with [him] while she was on her break.
'[Another colleague] reported to the investigation that she had put her head through the curtain to check on the complainant after [Mr Mateo] had left and that the complainant told her, "He just asked me if I want to be part of the mile-high club."'
A former British Airways steward sacked for asking a female colleague if she wanted to 'join the mile-high club' has won almost £30,000 for unfair dismissal
The woman was said to have been left 'upset and emotional' following the interaction, and said she did not want to work with Mr Mateo again.
'I was made to feel extremely uncomfortable, and my privacy was totally invaded,' she told the BA investigation.
The tribunal heard: '[BA] had a genuine belief that [Mr Mateo] had made a reference to the "mile-high club" in a conversation with the complainant while she was on a rest break, that he also did purposely touch the complainant's leg while she was on a rest break and that he did tell the complainant stories of a sexual nature regarding two ladies.
'[BA] says that it did and it still does concern it that [Mr Mateo] did this whilst he was positioning on a flight (not operating as a member of the crew).'
Mr Mateo worked as cabin crew for British Airways between September 2018 and July 2024 when he was fired.
Prior to his dismissal he had a clean disciplinary record and had received commendations for good service.
He received a basic annual salary of £21,833 as well as duty allowance and bar commission.
The tribunal was told that Mr Mateo was reported in March 2024 over his conduct during the flight.
Following his suspension in April 2024, he flew to the USA on a tourist visa to be with his wife who was working as a postdoctoral research fellow at New York University.
He eventually flew back to the UK in July 2024 following his sacking, before applying to be added to his wife's visa as a dependent. He was later given a work permit.
Outlining why BA's dismissal was deemed unfair, Employment Judge Anna Macey said: 'I concluded that the dismissal was substantively unfair because of the failure to conduct a reasonable investigation due to [BA] interviewing [Mr Mateo] before it had taken a full version of the events from the complainant and the lack of in-depth questioning by [BA] of the complainant concerning her allegation that [Mr Mateo] had touched her knee.'
Mr Mateo said he wanted to be reinstated to his former position but this was rejected by the tribunal.
Judge Macey said: 'I am satisfied that [BA] does have a genuine belief that trust and confidence has irretrievably broken down based on its genuine belief that [Mr Mateo] committed the allegations made by the complainant.
'These are serious allegations of harassment of a sexual nature.
'[BA] has a genuine and rational belief that [Mr Mateo] committed the allegations and its loss of trust and confidence is sufficient on its own to prevent re-employment because it is not practicable.
'I concluded at the liability hearing that [Mr Mateo] had disturbed the complainant while she was on her break behind a privacy curtain to conduct a non-work related conversation with the complainant.
'I concluded that this was blameworthy conduct. It was an invasion of the complainant's privacy and I agree that it was strange behaviour.
'There is insufficient evidence for me to conclude that [Mr Mateo] would repeat either the allegations [BA] genuinely believes that he committed or the blameworthy conduct that I concluded he had committed.'

Several hospitals in Siberia have been placed under quarantine after the death of a laboratory worker who was reportedly exposed to the highly contagious pneumonic plague .
Local media said Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old lab assistant, died in the early hours of 2 October - days after accidentally breaking a test tube containing the pathogen.
A number of hospitals were closed immediately and placed under a quarantine expected to last three weeks, while 200 people have been placed under strict medical observation, according to the independent Russian outlet Baikal People .
Russian authorities denied a link between the death and a lab leak despite multiple media reports.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Washington was monitoring the case closely, aware that "it could spread quickly" despite the quarantine and other public health protocols.
There have been conflicting reports over how Shipilova fell ill.
Baikal People said Shipilova was working with live biological material at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute on 25 September when she accidentally smashed a test tube containing the dangerous bacteria Yersinia pestis .
After two days, her condition is said to have deteriorated and she was rushed to the hospital. Doctors initially suspected she had coronavirus due to her symptoms and admitted her to a specialised Covid unit at the district hospital in Shelekhov.
She was put on a ventilator before she died on 2 October.
The response of authorities has been mixed, causing further confusion. Officials have said being that Shipilova died of “pneumonia of an unknown origin”.
Doctors in Irkutsk are “openly talking about plague”, according to Baikal People.
Euronews reports that Alexey Tsydenov, the governor of the neighbouring Buryatia region, said Shipilova’s death was linked to a plague infection but his statement was later changed to include the word “maybe”.
Baikalsk authorities also advised residents not to travel to Shelekhov on Saturday “due to unofficial information about a confirmed case of plague in a person in the city of Shelekhov”. The post was deleted less than two hours later.
Masks were also made compulsory as a preventive measure at the aluminium plant in Shelekhov on Saturday. Rospotrebnadzor, the national public health agency of the Russian Federation, has insisted that the situation in the region is “stable”.
According to its website, the institution was set up in 1934 by an order of the USSR with the intention of functioning as a “scientific operative body for plague control”. It is a state-run institution, although much of its work is tightly controlled.
Over the years it has expanded its work to other diseases including cholera, brucellosis, tularemia, anthrax, and arbovirus infections.
However, it also serves a possible national security function monitoring for data on “the amount of incidents suspicious to biological terrorism” in Siberia and the Far East since 2001.
The structure of the Institute is divided into three departments including an anti-epidemic division covering infections including anthrax and tularemia and plague microbiology and an experimental division with both a biochemical and pathophysiological subdivision.
There is also a research and production department and general purpose division, which covers information analytics including the purposes of “selection and summarising of national and foreign literature data on the directions of the Institute’s researches”, a lab for testing animals and lab for “experimental animals”.
Professional and advanced training is also offered.
According to analysis by Anthony Rimmington, a former Senior Research Fellow at Birmingham University, writing in February 2025 , much of Russia’s anti-plague work remains closed to the international community.
According to a statement by the US state department shared with Radio Free Liberty on Sunday , the US is “aware of reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in Irkutsk Oblast, Russia”.
“We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners,” it said.
It urged Russian authorities to “share accurate information quickly and openly.”
“Plague infections occur regularly with a few hundred cases a year globally,” Prof Paul Hunter, professor of medicine at the University of East Anglia told The Independent.
“There are different forms of the disease, bubonic and septicaemic are spread by flea bites from close contact with infected animals.
“Pneumonic plague is spread person to person through respiratory droplets. Laboratory acquired infections are not unknown and are usually acquired through inhalation hence pneumonic plague in lab worker, if that is what it is.”

articles.title_orig: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
articles.title_zh: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
articles.content_orig:
Wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse and its numbers dwindled across New Zealand due to predators and habitat loss
The population of New Zealand’s endemic wētāpunga – believed to be the world’s heaviest insect – is officially “increasing” thanks to a groundbreaking breeding programme that has overseen the release of 11,000 insects into the wild.
“The future of wētāpunga is looking bright,” said Dr Chris Green, an honorary researcher at the department of conservation, who documented the success of the project for the New Zealand Journal of Zoology. Green co-authored a report released on 2 October that outlines the success of the breeding programme.
“Eleven thousand individuals for release is extraordinary and outstanding.”
A female wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse. Its body can grow up to 10cm long (nearly 4in) and its leg span can be as wide as 20cm.
It is the largest of 70 wētā species and was once found across parts of the North Island before predation from introduced species and habitat loss contributed to their decline. By the 1990s, they were considered “endangered” and are now presumed extinct in the wild on New Zealand’s mainland. The insects reside primarily on a smattering of predator-free islands in Auckland’s Hauraki Gulf and off the coast of Northland.
But their fortune is starting to change. Over the past 15 years, tens of thousands of wētāpunga have been bred at Butterfly Creek, a wildlife facility, and Auckland zoo, enabling the release of wētāpunga across new predator-free islands and some mainland reserves north of Auckland.
Butterfly Creek and Auckland zoo established husbandry techniques that, over time, have been scaled up to rear large numbers of wētāpunga in communal creches. The young wētāpunga – or nymphs – are fed a three-part diet of fresh foliage, fish flake protein and leaf litter. The protein is “critical” to the survival of the youngest nymphs, Green said.
Once big enough to protect themselves, the insects are transferred to their new habitat. The efforts have led to 45 separate translocations to wild habitats, which is “a very high number in any recovery of a species”, Green said.
Monitoring on two islands has shown wētāpunga have established self-sustaining populations, with fourth and fifth generations born there, in what Green said was a marker of success. As a result, the species’ conservation status has improved from “nationally endangered” to “nationally increasing”.
“It’s so exciting, because we are unable to report that for so many of our other threatened species,” Green said.
New Zealand is particularly vulnerable to species decline because of its high rates of endemism and problems with introduced pests.
Green said the country was at the forefront of invertebrate recovery work and he was not aware of any other examples of breeding programmes working to this scale, or with such success.
By documenting the project’s work, he hopes other institutions will feel encouraged to develop their own programmes.
“That’s the extraordinary aspect of it – that we’ve been successful,” he said. “If other institutions can get into that sort of position, then there can be huge benefit for threatened species in New Zealand.”

articles.title_orig: Karl Deisseroth wins Nobel Prize
articles.title_zh: Karl Deisseroth wins Nobel Prize
articles.content_orig:
Nobel Prize-winning American researcher Karl Deisseroth is a psychiatrist, neuroscientist and bioengineer who has spent more than two decades illuminating the workings of the brain to unlock its mysteries.
The Stanford University scientist spoke to AFP about the Nobel Prize in medicine, which was awarded on Monday, for his work in optogenetics -- a technique combining light and genetics -- alongside German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel.
The trio were honored "for their discovery of a molecular switch for nerve cells," the Nobel Assembly said.
- What is the advantage of your approach? -
"This is a long-sought goal in neuroscience because the brain is so complicated with billions of cells that are next to each other and do completely different things," Deisseroth told AFP.
"We needed a way to resolve them, to control one without affecting the other. And the way to do that, as it turns out, is to take something that they normally don't respond to at all, which is light, and give the capability to just some of the cells to respond to light.
"And then, you've got a great way to be specific."
- How does this work change psychiatry? -
Using light, researchers are now able to switch individual neural circuits on or off in a brain.
They have also been able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders.
"Unlike most other fields of medicine, in psychiatry we haven't had a good model for what's actually different," Deisseroth said.
"In cardiology, we can model everything about all the diverse symptoms of heart failure by looking at the heart as a failing pump. It's not pumping as well, and we can quantify how badly it's pumping.
"With the brain, we haven't had that. We haven't had a measurable that we can say, 'Oh, this part is not working well enough.'
"In psychiatry it's been a problem, and optogenetics has started to address that because we can say, 'these cells are too active' or 'not active enough,' and that guides us in a very powerful way."
- Is there a potential therapeutic effect? -
"Once you know the cells that are involved, you can study those cells, see which medications or which drugs that cell might respond to, and then you can test those medications in a way that really cuts through a lot of the guesswork in clinical trials," Deisseroth said, adding "that is exciting because it's much more general."
"And there are big clinical trials now that have come out of phase II and entering the final phase, phase III of clinical trials, based on indirect optogenetics for autism and for schizophrenia that are looking promising."
- What cound such treatments do for patients? -
"I'll give an example with autism. There are treatments, medications that are currently given for irritability in autism -- that's the syndrome of aggression and irritated discontrol that people with autism can have that causes a lot of trouble.
"So, what do we do with that now? All we have are very, very strong medications that are called antipsychotics. These are medications that cause a lot of weight gain, a lot of sedation. They cause abnormal movements, a lot of side effects, but they're still used because people are so desperate for help.
"Now, what's going into phase III studies is a non-antipsychotic for irritability in autism. It's completely different."
Deisseroth offered another example with Parkinson's disease, a progressive brain disorder that can cause shaking, stiffness and difficulty controlling movement.
"Parkinson's is a very interesting disorder because there's death of a kind of neuron called a dopamine neuron. But dopamine neurons do a lot of different things in the brain. They affect planning. They affect movement. They affect reward or pleasure. They affect vomiting. They affect nursing. All these different things.
"And so our medications for Parkinson's cause a lot of problems because you're driving dopamine action in all these different domains, and it causes trouble.
"Our hope is with optogenetics we'll get more specific treatments, so we just affect, for example, movement, which is a primary problem in Parkinson's."
- What does this mean for neurotech devices? -
"Brain-computer interfaces are largely implemented with electricity. So there, there's electrical recording of activity, and in some cases, if activity is fed back in, there's electrical stimulation as well.
"Optical methods in principle provide another way for communication to happen. You can use, in principle, light instead of electricity. I would say that this as a potential application is a bit more farther out, though. It's an interesting thing, but one that probably will take a little time to build."

articles.title_orig: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.title_zh: World Space Week: Which countries have sent people to space?
articles.content_orig:
Sixty-nine years ago this day, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first satellite to orbit Earth, opening the Space Age and setting off a race with the United States.
Ten years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty came into force.
In 1999, the United Nations started observing World Space Week – from October 4 to 10 – to celebrate the contribution of space technology for the benefit of humanity. Schools, space agencies, museums and astronomy clubs around the world hold stargazing nights, science classes, exhibitions and talks by astronauts and scientists.
Today, more than 80 countries have put satellites into orbit, and people from over 50 of those have travelled to space.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at which countries have done so, how many space travellers have been women, and what comes next for human spaceflight.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet astronaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space.
On board the Vostok 1 spacecraft, he completed one orbit of Earth at about 27,400km/h (17,025mph) during a 108-minute flight. He later ejected from the spacecraft and landed by parachute.
The mission demonstrated that humans could survive launch, weightlessness and re-entry, giving the Soviet Union a major early victory in the Cold War Space Race.
Six years later, on October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty entered into force. Signed by the US, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union, it established that space should be explored and used peacefully and that no country could claim it as territory.
Less than two years later, NASA’s Apollo 11 mission landed the first humans on the moon. On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on its surface.
There is no single agreed boundary for where space begins: most international bodies use the Karman line, 100km (62 miles) above Earth, while the US military, NASA and the Federal Aviation Administration count anyone who flies above 80km (50 miles).
Either way, it is closer than it sounds: if Earth were the size of an apple, space would begin about as far from the surface as the thickness of its skin.
By the Karman line measure, at least 746 people from 52 countries have travelled to space, including professional astronauts and paying tourists.
Some hold dual nationality, and some flew for countries that no longer exist, such as the Soviet Union.
The graphic below breaks down space travellers by country.
Two countries still dominate the list. The US has sent 369 people to space, and the Soviet Union and Russia have sent 138 combined. China, the third country to launch people on its own rockets, has sent 29.
Space remains a male-dominated frontier. Science fiction may be full of women commanding starships, but of the 746 people who have travelled to space, only 112, or 15 percent, have been women, about one in seven.
Soviet astronaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman to travel to space in June 1963. The US did not follow for another 20 years, until Sally Ride flew in June 1983.
The share of women is rising, though, largely because of commercial flights. More than half of the women who have flown since 2020 went up as paying passengers or guests on Blue Origin’s suborbital rocket.
Most people who have flown to space were in their 30s or 40s on their first flight, which together account for 85 percent. The median age is 40. Commercial flights have widened that range.
The youngest traveller, Oliver Daemen, was 18 when he flew in 2021. The oldest, Ed Dwight, was 90 years and eight months old when he flew in 2024, about two months older than William Shatner had been on his flight three years earlier.
In April 2026, the Artemis II crew flew around the moon and reached about 406,771km (252,756 miles) from Earth, breaking the distance record set by Apollo 13 in 1970.
Next is Artemis III in 2027, a rehearsal in Earth orbit to test docking with lunar landers built by SpaceX and Blue Origin. NASA is targeting 2028 for Artemis IV, which aims to land astronauts near the moon’s south pole, the first crewed landing since 1972.
India plans its first crewed Gaganyaan flight in 2027, making it the fourth country to launch people on its own rocket. China aims to land astronauts on the moon around 2030.

The Supreme Court on Monday opened its new term by hearing arguments in a lawsuit filed in state court by the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, seeking to hold two major energy companies responsible for their alleged role in climate change and its impact. After nearly two hours of debate in Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County , it wasn’t clear whether a majority of the justices agreed with the energy companies that federal law prohibits Boulder’s claims. With Justice Samuel Alito recused from the dispute, a 4-4 tie would leave the ruling by the Colorado Supreme Court, allowing Boulder’s case to move forward, in place.
Monday’s argument was the latest chapter in an eight-year-old battle that began when Boulder filed a lawsuit in a state court in Colorado against two energy companies: Suncor, a subsidiary of one of Canada’s largest energy companies, which operates the only two oil refineries in Colorado; and ExxonMobil, the largest energy company in the United States. It is seeking compensation for some of the costs that it has incurred as a result of the alleged effects of climate change – for example, protecting its own property as well as that of its residents. Boulder contends that both energy companies have long deceived the public about the effects of climate change and the role of fossil-fuel products in creating those effects; it also contended that the companies played a role in climate change by producing, refining, and marketing fossil fuels.
After their efforts to move the case to federal court failed, the energy companies asked the state trial court to dismiss the case, but it turned down that request. The Colorado Supreme Court then agreed to decide whether Boulder’s state-law claims were trumped by federal law. It concluded that they were not, and its claims could go forward. The companies came to the Supreme Court last year, asking the justices to weigh in, which they agreed in February to do.
Representing the energy companies, lawyer Kannon Shanmugam described Boulder’s claims as an “unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct.” The Constitution, he said, bars the application of state law to “certain inherently federal areas,” and the Supreme Court has long held that federal law governs interstate-pollution claims. Moreover, he added, a state cannot regulate out-of-state conduct “based solely on attenuated effects” that it might have within the state.
Chief Justice John Roberts appeared skeptical, however. He suggested to both Shanmugam and Sarah Harris, the principal deputy U.S. solicitor general who argued on behalf of the Trump administration in support of the energy companies, that it was not uncommon for lawsuits to be based on conduct that occurs outside a state but has broad “effects,” including within the state. He asked Harris “what makes this situation different from those” other cases in which the court allowed lawsuits to proceed in state court.
Harris answered that, unlike those lawsuits, Colorado would ban the production of fossil fuels anywhere in the country.
Roberts did not appear persuaded. “That’s a question of relief” for Colorado, “and what might be available,” he said. It did not, in his view, necessarily seem to go to the question of whether Colorado could bring the lawsuit at all.
Justice Elena Kagan also seemed dubious of the energy companies’ arguments. She told Shanmugam that Boulder’s “suit appears to be based on the old 1990s tobacco suits,” as well as more recent lawsuits against opioid manufacturers. Were those lawsuits also trumped by federal law, she asked?
Shanmugam pushed back, describing the tobacco and opioid lawsuits as different. He stressed that the injury at the center of Boulder’s case “is not suffered by the Colorado consumer in the traditional sense.” He then pointed back to the principle that federal law has traditionally applied to claims involving interstate air and water pollution.
Kagan remained doubtful, asking Shanmugam to point to the support for that argument in the text of the Constitution or federal law or in the Supreme Court’s cases. “Where,” she finally asked, “is the[re] anything for that?”
Representing Boulder, lawyer Kevin Russell echoed Roberts’ point, telling the justices that states have long had the power to provide court remedies for injuries that occur within their borders even when the conduct that caused those injuries occurred elsewhere. Applying state law, he said, has never been interpreted as projecting that law nationwide. And he emphasized that Congress has the authority to pass laws that preempt state laws if and when it wants to.
Russell faced tough questioning, however, from Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was the member of the court most supportive of the energy companies’ position. He pointed to a series of Supreme Court cases that, in his words, “make crystal-clear that interstate air and water pollution are matters for federal law” unless Congress specifies otherwise. In Kavanaugh’s view, those cases mean that state law generally does not apply to claims like Boulder’s, and Congress could believe that interstate-pollution issues are federal issues – and that it therefore does not need to pass new legislation to say so explicitly.
Several justices expressed concern about the possibility that allowing Boulder’s lawsuit to go forward would open the floodgates to even more cases in other states around the country. Justice Clarence Thomas asked Russell to describe any principles that might restrict whom state and local governments could sue.
Russell cited constraints on a state’s jurisdiction over particular defendants and a constitutional doctrine (known as the dormant commerce clause) that bars states from discriminating against out-of-state defendants, among other things, as possible limiting principles.
That prompted Thomas to ask whether, under Boulder’s theory, state and local governments could also sue “large retailers” of fossil fuels.
Russell acknowledged that “[n]othing in our theory prevents that,” but he added that “when lots of people act together to cause widespread harm, it is not uncommon for multiple different defendants to be potentially liable.”
Justice Amy Coney Barrett also sought to test the limits of Boulder’s theory, asking Russell whether Colorado could pass a law that sought to cap greenhouse-gas emissions in the other 49 states as well.
Russell agreed that such a law would be prohibited and sought to distinguish that scenario from Boulder’s lawsuit. He emphasized that, with the lawsuit, Boulder wasn’t trying to directly regulate the energy companies’ actions. The lawsuit, he argued, “doesn’t prohibit them from engaging in the conduct.” Instead, he said, “[i]t requires them to internalize a portion of the cost of their activities by paying for some of the damage that those activities inflict.”
Shanmugam picked up on these concerns in his rebuttal, telling the court that the “breadth of Boulder’s theory here is astonishing.” Indeed, he suggested, it would mean that on an upcoming visit to Colorado, Boulder could sue him “for refilling my car and thereby contributing to global climate change.” Moreover, he suggested, it would not be only state and local governments who could sue under Boulder’s theory, but “[a]ny individual who has suffered the effects of climate change.” “Climate change,” he concluded, “is certainly one of the most pressing issues of the day, but we would submit that this is exactly the wrong way to go about resolving it.”
However the court opts to resolve the case, the justices devoted relatively little time to whether the Supreme Court has the power to consider the energy companies’ appeal at all – a question that the justices had asked the litigants to address when they agreed to take up the case earlier this year. articles.title_orig: Hochul Declares a Measles Emergency as Cases Rise in Rural New York
articles.title_zh: Hochul Declares a Measles Emergency as Cases Rise in Rural New York
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK (WABC) -- Governor Kathy Hochul has issued an executive order on Monday declaring a State Disaster Emergency in response to the growing number of measles cases across rural areas of New York and neighboring states.
As of October 3, there have been seven confirmed cases in New York City and 101 in New York State outside of of the city, for 108 total cases this year, amid a global and domestic increase in measles cases.
Since July 15, there have been 92 cases reported among under-immunized, rural communities in 18 counties.
Since then, local health departments have administered over 1,000 doses of the MMR vaccine across rural areas of New York State.
The executive order signed on Monday expands the network of vaccine administrators to add paramedics, advanced EMS, midwives and pharmacists.
"After reviewing the latest data on measles cases in New York State, I am declaring a State Disaster Emergency to strengthen our ongoing efforts to confront this disease," Governor Hochul said. "No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease. That is why I have taken steps to increase the number of health professionals who can vaccinate and test. These emergency measures will protect New Yorkers and support our community partners as they work tirelessly to address the spread of this disease."
The governor received her flu shot on Monday and is urging all New Yorkers to do the same.

articles.title_orig: In a divided world, St. Francis points the way forward
articles.title_zh: In a divided world, St. Francis points the way forward
articles.content_orig:
Author: Br. Murray Bodo, OFM
Date Published: October 05, 2026
In declaring 2026 the year of St. Francis , Pope Leo has once again called attention to the depth and breadth of the world’s interest in St. Francis. In this, the 800th anniversary year of his death , Francis has emerged as a saint who is as relevant today as he was in his lifetime.
We live in a time of division and upheaval in the world, with wars cropping up in the Middle East and Eastern Europe, and with hateful rhetoric and divisive decisions that are separating people. The good among us are longing and praying for peace daily: peace in the world and peace of heart. We long for models and look to saints for guidance about how we are to live our lives. Again and again, we turn to Francis of Assisi as the Christian example of a peacemaker who found peace of heart and preached peace and good by embracing Jesus and His Gospel of Peace and Love. “May the Lord give you peace,” and “Peace and Good” were the two mantras that Francis uttered his whole life long.
Ours is also a time of turmoil in nature. Our climate is warming yearly, and the excessive human consumption and use of fossil fuels are damaging our planet. There is the feeling that we are pushing the envelope of what our climate can take of human neglect and abuse.
And again, it is Francis of Assisi who emerges as a model of what it means to embrace all of creation as our brothers and sisters through whom and with whom we make our way to God. For St. Francis, it is because of the Incarnation of God among us that all creatures are redeemed, all creatures are seen as good. Francis embraced all creatures and called them Brothers and Sisters; and towards the end of his life he sang one of the great poems of the Middle Ages and of all time, his “Canticle of the Creatures.”
“Laudato si, mi Signore,” St. Francis sings, “Praised be You, my Lord,” through Brother Sun and Moon and the Stars; through Mother Earth, our Sister; through Brother Wind and Air, Brother Fire and Sister Water. In so taking the four elements of Medieval Cosmology: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire, and embracing them and praising God through, with, and in them, St. Francis was embracing all creatures of the earth and praising and thanking God for them.
St. Francis of Assisi is the patron of ecology. (Photo courtesy of Br. Octavio Duran, OFM)
What a program for a renewal of the earth! What a program for peace of heart and peace among people and all creatures. And in his pursuit of that program for a peace-filled world, Pope Francis turned to St. Francis’s “Canticle” for the title and framework of his encyclical “Laudato Si,” in which Pope Francis stated that the most pressing need of the environment today is to address the human and social roots of the ecological crisis. For example, the encyclical calls for an immediate transition away from fossil fuels because climate change disproportionately affects the poor. Also, the wealthy consume and pollute excessively while the poor suffer the gravest consequences of environmental degradation, often being denied basic human rights like clean water.
The deepest crisis identified by “Laudato Si” is the placing of technology and economic profit above all else. Therefore, the most critical need of the world today is a profound and spiritual change that would lead to a more integrated vision of human beings, of their life, and their relationship with nature.
What a universal patron saint for these profound changes in our times is St. Francis! It has been suggested that the month of October, the month of his passing, be dedicated to St. Francis of Assisi, who is already a universal icon of peace and love among us. Perhaps Franciscans could ask that favor of Pope Leo, could suggest that we need to be reminded every year of the gift we have in St. Francis for renewing relationships in our time: the relationship we have with ourselves, with others, and with the very planet we live upon. All people need to hear every year St. Francis’s Admonition to his brothers who would be peacemakers:
“The peace which you proclaim with words must dwell even more abundantly in your hearts. Do not provoke others to anger or give scandal. Rather, let your gentleness draw them to peace, goodness and concord. This is our vocation: to heal wounds, to bind what is broken, to bring home those who are lost.” (Legend of the Three Companions, 58)

articles.title_orig: Trump approves firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter, Pentagon says
articles.title_zh: Trump approves firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter, Pentagon says
articles.content_orig:
Nidal Hasan sentenced to death by military jury in 2013 for carrying out deadly shooting attack at army base in Texas
Donald Trump has approved the execution by US army firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who was sentenced to death for killing 13 soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a social media post.
Hasan, who was an army psychiatrist, would become the first US soldier to be executed by the US military in more than 60 years.
Parnell said in a post on X that defense secretary Pete Hegseth “has recommended – and President Donald J. Trump has approved – death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan”.
He added: “The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come.”
Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 for carrying out the mass shooting at the Fort Hood base.
He chose to conduct his own defense during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges. Court-appointed defense attorneys expressed concern that he was seeking execution.
Hasan, a US-born Muslim of Palestinian descent, opened fire on 5 November 2009 at a medical facility in the sprawling military base, which served as a staging point for soldiers to deploy to combat zones in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Twelve of the dead and 30 of the wounded were soldiers. Hasan was shot and partially paralyzed by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack.
The court that convicted Hasan was told that he was opposed to the US military’s occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that Hasan had spoken online with the radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, an al-Qaida propagandist and American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.
Although US mass shootings are disturbingly common, they are rare at military facilities.
In 2025, a soldier opened fire at a US military base in the state of Georgia, wounding five fellow troops before he was tackled and apprehended.
In 2019, a US sailor fatally shot two people and wounded a third at a base in Hawaii, while a Saudi military student shot dead three people at a military facility in Florida the same year.
A Kuwaiti-born US citizen attacked two military installations in Tennessee in 2015, killing four Marines and a sailor. The FBI concluded the violence was inspired by a “foreign terrorist group.”
Two years earlier, a man killed 12 people and wounded eight at the Washington Navy Yard in the US capital before being shot dead by officers.

articles.title_orig: Alleged Chinese agent accused of surveilling Taiwanese president's son appears in federal court
articles.title_zh: Alleged Chinese agent accused of surveilling Taiwanese president's son appears in federal court
articles.content_orig:
A suspected Chinese agent appeared in a Los Angeles federal court Monday after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's son near Seattle last year.
Orange County, California, realtor Wanying "Heather" Zhang, 34, appeared calm, dressed in a tailored, white zip-up jacket, sweatpants and white sneakers, with shackles on her wrists and ankles. CBS News was first to report that the FBI arrested Zhang on Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China.
In court, she spoke only to confirm her name and that she understood the charge against her of working as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government.
Zhang was represented by a public defender at the hearing.
Judge Steve Kim rescheduled her detention hearing to Wednesday to give Zhang more time to hire a private criminal defense attorney.
Zhang was remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals until her Wednesday hearing.
The public defender, Chad Pennington, told the judge he believed Zhang intended to hire private counsel.
Her husband, Edric Ding, watched the proceedings, flanked by his sister, attorney Elaine Lori.
Standing at the podium, Zhang looked back at her husband briefly, but showed no emotion.
Lori and Ding declined to comment inside the courthouse and remained silent as they were questioned by reporters as they walked to their car after the hearing. When reached by phone on Sunday, Ding told CBS News, "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.
Three prosecutors represented the Justice Department: Scott Lara of the National Security Division's Counterintelligence and Export Control Section, and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Amanda Elbogen and Colin Scott. They said they were not authorized to comment.
U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli posted a video on X of Zhang being frogmarched through the airport by federal law enforcement on Sunday, wearing the same outfit she wore in court on Monday.
A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of allegedly traveling to Seattle in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.
Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.
Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.
The FBI agent's affidavit claimed the government obtained text messages between Zhang and Chinese government officials evidencing the alleged surveillance.
In one exchange, Zhang allegedly texted her supposed Chinese government handler on the day of her alleged Seattle trip, "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," while footage from Ting-Yu's neighbor's security camera showed her "appearing to film" the president's son, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening, according to the affidavit.
As well as arresting Zhang on Sunday, FBI agents also searched her home in an upscale suburb of Irvine, California.
A resident of the neighborhood said she saw about 10 FBI agents searching Zhang's home on Sunday morning.
"Several of them were sitting at a table inside the garage," said the neighbor, who asked to remain anonymous due to safety concerns. "Even the ones standing guard were wearing gloves. They told us there was a search going on."
Zhang appears to have been renting the home, after selling her 6,030-square-foot, six-bed house a mile away for $6 million in June, according to property records.
A former neighbor told CBS News he was surprised that the young realtor couple could afford such an expensive property.
"She introduced herself as Heather," said the neighbor, who also asked to remain anonymous due to safety concerns. "She was super friendly.
"Usually, the people here, they're a little bit older, because the price of the homes is from $3 million to $10 million. But they were very young," the neighbor continued. "They did a lot of upgrades. Even though the house was almost brand new, they started changing so many things."
"Two years later, they only sold it for a little bit higher than what they purchased. It didn't make sense why would they want to lose money after spending all of that money," the neighbor added.
The Justice Department claims Zhang was working as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government from June 2025 to September 2025, and plotted her surveillance mission with Beijing officials during a trip to China in June 2025.
"The complaint in this case lays bare a brazen plot directed by the Chinese government to conduct a covert surveillance mission on U.S. soil targeting close relatives of a Taiwanese government official," Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division said in a statement released Monday.
"Wanying Zhang's arrest for allegedly acting as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government makes clear how far China's authoritarian regime will go to advance its goals. However, this case also demonstrates the FBI's unwavering commitment to defending the sovereignty of our democratic allies and combating all attempts by the Chinese government - and any foreign adversary - to conduct transnational repression within our borders," Rozhavsky said.
The Chinese and Taiwanese governments have not responded to requests for comment.

articles.title_orig: I won't accept exclusion, says Polanski after criticism of Zionism motion
articles.title_zh: I won't accept exclusion, says Polanski after criticism of Zionism motion
articles.content_orig:
Zack Polanski has said he will not accept anyone being excluded from the Green Party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of", after members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.
The Green leader said "no-one will be made unwelcome because of their background, their faith, or where they worship".
The motion defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".
More than a dozen Labour MPs reported the Greens to the equality watchdog on Monday, saying it raised "serious questions".
A Green Party spokesperson said: "We remain committed to upholding our own Code of Conduct and our duties under the Equality Act, and to ensuring the Green Party continues to be a safe place for all members."
Nine Labour MPs have also referred the party to Sussex Police, asking the force to investigate whether alleged "possible antisemitic offences" at the conference merit a criminal investigation.
Sussex Police has been contacted for comment.
It is the latest development in a backlash to the policy motion , which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton and endorsed by 1,022 votes to 813.
"The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it said.
The motion has exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under leader Zack Polanski and its MPs elected at the last general election.
Polanski did not take part in the vote on Sunday and four of the party's five MPs opposed it.
Israel's foreign ministry responded by banning Polanski from entering the country, while some Jewish groups have described it as an "attack on the Jewish community".
In his first comments since the motion was passed, having declined interviews on Monday, Polanski released a lengthy statement saying he "take[s] seriously my responsibility to make sure everyone feels safe and welcome in our party".
He added: "As leader I will not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of."
He said his party and its leadership stood for "deeply held values of compassion, fairness and equality for all".
Polanski, who is Jewish, added that "antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct".
On Monday, a group of Labour MPs wrote two letters to the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) - organised by former Home Office minister Mike Tapp - raising concerns about the motion, and amendments to protect Jewish members attending Zionist synagogues being voted down.
"Taken together, these developments raise serious questions about whether Jewish members can participate freely and equally in the party, and whether their religious and communal connections could expose them to complaints or disciplinary action," their letter to the watchdog said.
The EHRC, which regulates equality law in Great Britain, previously found failings in how Labour handled antisemitism.
In a statement, the EHRC told the BBC it would "consider each complaint carefully" and had not at this stage launched an investigation.
It added: "We have guidance advising political parties on their responsibilities under the Equality Act 2010. Like all duty-bearers, political parties must comply with the Act and take steps to avoid discrimination."
The European Green Party, of which the Green Party for England and Wales is a member, released a statement on Monday saying it wanted to "unequivocally distance" itself from the motion.
The umbrella body said it would "immediately demand clarity" from the party's leadership on how they would protect Jewish people and self-determination.
Meanwhile, Green MP Ellie Chowns told Radio 4's PM programme she was "deeply saddened" the motion had become party policy but disagreed it was antisemitic, saying it was underpinned by "principled opposition to the actions of the Israeli government".
She suggested a review of Green policymaking processes was needed since "less than 1%" of the party's more than 200,000 members had participated in the vote.

articles.title_orig: Yemen war: What’s the latest, as government forces claim advances?
articles.title_zh: Yemen war: What’s the latest, as government forces claim advances?
articles.content_orig:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has announced a major military campaign to retake all territory controlled by the Houthis, marking a new escalation in a civil war that had largely been frozen for several years before battles intensified in recent weeks.
The announcement by Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), the executive body of the Yemeni government, comes after weeks of heavy fighting and major Houthi advances along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the strategically important city of Taiz.
On Monday, Yemeni government forces said they were launching a “strategic” offensive on the country’s capital, Sanaa, which the Houthis have held since 2014.
Earlier in the day, the Yemeni forces — who are backed by Saudi Arabia — said they had regained control of the Dhubab district on the country’s west coast near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, though the Houthis denied the announcement. The Yemeni government later said it had also captured the port city of Mocha.
The fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah, meaning Supporters of God in Arabic – and Yemeni government forces has expanded since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July, displacing more than 100,000 people since then.
Last month, the Houthis launched a rapid offensive that captured about 150km (93 miles) of Red Sea coastline and areas around Bab al-Mandeb, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, which is a critical route for international shipping.
On Monday, the foreign minister of Yemen’s internationally recognised government requested more support from the international community to defeat the Houthis, saying it is “in the world’s interest” for the country to be stable.
“We call upon our brothers, friends and the international community to support the Yemeni people, their state, and their national institutions in confronting the terrorist Houthi militia, which seizes their will by force of arms and lays waste to the lives of their sons – after exhausting all opportunities for de-escalation and peace,” Afrah al-Zouba said in a post on X.
So what is the latest on the fighting, and what does Yemen’s government hope to achieve?
The Yemeni government army said on Monday 1,747 Houthi fighters had been “neutralised” in 1,122 military operations in the Saada, al-Jawf and Taiz governorates and along Yemen’s western coast.
Military spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili said the attacks targeted artillery and rocket positions, fortifications, supply lines, reinforcements and command centres.
Al-Nuzaili said warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers were involved and 364 military and logistical vehicles had been destroyed or disabled. The casualty and equipment figures could not be independently verified.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government also announced that its forces had taken control of Dhubab and Mocha on the Red Sea coast and were launching a major offensive on Sanaa.
Elsewhere, the front line in Marib governorate in northeastern Yemen witnessed an escalation in fighting on Monday.
A military source told Al Jazeera that government forces launched an attack on Houthi positions on the Raghwan front in the north of the governorate, coinciding with air raids on Houthi positions and reinforcements.
The source said the raids targeted Houthi positions near Mount Helan as well as an arms depot and military reinforcements northwest of Marib.
On Sunday, a Saudi-led coalition said its forces carried out 97 attacks against Houthi reinforcements around Taiz and the Tor al-Baha front using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers.
On the developments in Taiz, Al Jazeera’s Yemen bureau chief, Saeed Thabet, said Houthi operations in the rural areas around the strategic city are based on guerrilla tactics aimed at easing pressure on the coastal front and tightening the blockade of the road to Aden.
Al-Alimi said on Sunday that government forces had been ordered to launch military operations to regain Houthi-controlled territory and restore state authority across Yemen.
“We have instructed the armed forces, security forces and all military formations to begin carrying out their assigned tasks under an approved plan until the country is liberated from the Houthis,” al-Alimi said.
Military sources told the Reuters news agency that over the previous 48 hours, the Houthis advanced against government and local forces on strategic hilltops near Taiz, pushing forward along the last remaining road linking the city with Aden on Yemen’s southern coast. The AFP news agency quoted four security sources as saying the Houthis had cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden, the Yemeni government’s interim capital.
The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and much of Yemen’s populous northwest since 2014. Saudi Arabia intervened militarily the following year at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognised government but failed to dislodge the group.
A United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 brought years of relative calm before fighting intensified again this year. The latest round of fighting has focused heavily on the Red Sea coast and Taiz.
Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemeni defence analyst, said he believes the government and its allies face a formidable rival in the Houthis.
The missile arsenal of the Houthis, the precision of their drones and military “capabilities have grown” with support from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), he told Al Jazeera.
Having joined the US-Israel war on Iran on their own timeline, the Houthis have reinforced their place in Tehran’s “axis of resistance” and given the IRGC a way to shift pressure from the Strait of Hormuz to Bab al-Mandeb in the Red Sea, he said.
Saudi Arabia has pledged continued support for the internationally recognised government.
Coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki said Saudi Arabia and its allies would continue supporting Yemen until state institutions were restored and the Houthi threat to shipping in the southern Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb was ended.
Al-Maliki said Saudi Arabia had an “inherent right” to defend its sovereignty and take military measures to deter Houthi offensives, citing attacks in Riyadh, Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan, Najran, Taif and Yanbu in recent weeks.

articles.title_orig: Jeffrey Archer, Novelist Whose Real Life Rivaled His Thrillers, Dies at 86
articles.title_zh: Jeffrey Archer, Novelist Whose Real Life Rivaled His Thrillers, Dies at 86
articles.content_orig:
Jake Kerridge has been The Telegraph's Chief Obituary Writer since 2025. He has reviewed books for The Telegraph for more than 20 years and interviewed authors ranging from Margaret Atwood to Elmore Leonard.
Jeffrey Archer’s recent announcement of his retirement from writing was a blow for millions of readers around the world; his sudden death will compound their sadness . Although for the past quarter of a century he lived a much quieter life than in the days when his various non-literary activities – political, charitable, criminal – kept him in the media spotlight, he remained one of Britain’s bestselling authors until he died , even without the benefit of the blaring publicity of his heyday.
This was not because of any championing by literary tastemakers. Dame Jilly Cooper once observed that: “Jeffrey Archer and I long for a kind word in the Guardian, while literary writers have lots and lots of kind words in the Guardian but probably long for Jeffrey’s and my sales.” But where even Dame Jilly had achieved a measure of critical respectability by the time of her death a year ago, Lord Archer had to remain content with the sales.
Archer remained a byword for bad writing, an easy punchline. “Something smells evil,” observes an angel in Aziraphale’s bookshop, in a 2019 episode of the fantasy drama Good Omens. “Oh, that would be the Jeffrey Archer books, I’m afraid,” Aziraphale (Michael Sheen) replies.
To his critics, Archer simply could not write a decent sentence. “It is a very long book. To anyone who cares for language and literature it seems like the longest book in the world,” Paul Bailey declared of Archer’s Collected Short Stories in The Telegraph in 1997. “This reviewer, bored with the predictable ‘twists in the tale’, began to count the clichés for distraction and soon reached 400.”
How, then, do you explain all those adoring readers, and the phenomenal sales of more than 300 million books? The answer, his detractors say, is that he had a genius for publicity rather than a genius for literature. At the start of his writing career, he formed a brilliant partnership with his fearsome publisher Eddie Bell: Archer schmoozed his sales team, Mr Bell threatened them, with the result that Archer’s books were piled high in the shops.
Archer, frankly admitting that he was nowhere near the league of Graham Greene, noted nevertheless in 1982 that he was at No. 1 on the bestseller lists while Greene languished at No. 17 – “Because he won’t go out and promote his books like I do. I can’t understand it.” And now, in dying a matter of hours before the release of his novel Adam and Eve – a Second World War saga that he declared would be his last book because it was so good that he “could never hope to equal it again” – he has pulled off his last and perhaps greatest publicity coup.
And yet there was more to Archer’s success than blowing his own trumpet. His readers genuinely responded to his deliciously melodramatic plots, the outlandish coincidences, the globetrotting intrigue, the climactic courtroom scenes, the hints of insider knowledge. (He went to stay with the deputy director of the FBI when researching Shall We Tell the President?).
These readers came to cherish the way in which the heroines all speak to the heroes in an identical, archly mocking fashion (based, it is widely assumed, on the way in which Archer’s wife Mary communicated with him), and gladly followed Archer wherever he took them. In one of his short stories, a character is reading a book which, though its title is not mentioned, is identifiable as Archer’s own novel First Among Equals: “He became so engrossed in the story that he didn’t look up again until he had turned the last page.” Archer could get away with that little bit of self-puffery because it reflected the true experience of so many readers.
Archer freely admitted that he turned to writing to make money. In 1974 he found himself £500,000 in debt through misguided investments and felt obliged to step down as an MP. He wrote the first draft of a thriller, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less, in six weeks, in the desperate hope of making a couple of thousand pounds. In fact his first two novels made him a million pounds between them, while his third, Kane and Abel, remains one of the bestselling books of all time.
And yet once he had earned enough money to pay off his debts and then some, he found himself “hooked on writing”. The very fact that he wrote so many volumes of short stories – never a profitable venture for any writer – shows that his motives for writing were not merely mercenary.
He saw himself not as a fancy stylist but as an unostentatious craftsman like Somerset Maugham, and took real pains over his books, writing at least 14 drafts of every novel. In 2009 he even spent nine months rewriting Kane and Abel 30 years after its first publication, to give it the benefit of everything he had learnt as a writer in the interim. He never rested on his laurels, embarking on an ambitious eight-book series about a detective called William Warwick as he entered his eighties.
His readers sensed that if his sentences were not perfect, nor were they dashed off: here was a writer giving them 100 per cent. It is an odd word to associate with Jeffrey Archer, perhaps, but his novels radiated sincerity. They were not written for a market but truly reflected his own interests, foibles and values. Perhaps, above all else, the ineffably decent, straight-bat English heroes of his novels resonated with readers because their creator valued them so much – perhaps intending them as avatars of himself, or rather the type of man he would have liked to be.
I suspect Jeffrey Archer was the sort of author Dame Mary Beard was thinking of when she said recently, in her role as chairman of the Booker Prize judges, that she dislikes the idea that people “love reading”, when the purpose of books is to discomfit you and upset your world-view. Archer has never upset anybody’s world-view, but he has given millions of people a good time by creating a world more exciting and suspenseful than our own – and if it is not a very morally complex world, that makes the books even more effective as a source of solace and comfort.
Ask yourself: would you rather be stuck on a desert island with Dame Mary’s approved reading list or a suitcaseful of Archer novels? Archer may have done much in his life to merit full-blooded mockery, but as a writer he deserves more than back-handed compliments. It was a rackety life, but the pleasure he gave to so many people ought to count as a pretty considerable redemption.

articles.title_orig: Facing Backlash, Trump Says His Super PAC Will Pay for Taxpayer-Funded Ads
articles.title_zh: Facing Backlash, Trump Says His Super PAC Will Pay for Taxpayer-Funded Ads
articles.content_orig:
In a major reversal, President Donald Trump said Monday that he and his super PAC will now pay for campaign-style ads that promote his administration, instead of using federal funds .
Trump made the announcement on Truth Social after intense criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, some of whom questioned the legality of using taxpayer dollars for pro-Trump ads.
“The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”
Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., did not immediately respond to an inquiry about whether Trump and it would reimburse the government for the ads that have already aired. The White House did not answer that question, either.
“MAGA Inc. will pay for the PSA ads moving forward,” a White House official said.
“Presidential Public service announcements are nothing new. Administrations of both parties have used public service announcements to explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction,” the official added.
AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm, estimated the government has spent at least $10 million to air the ads.
The ads, which portray Trump in a favorable light, included disclaimers saying they were paid for by the U.S. government. One of the spots was virtually identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad.
NBC News reported last week that the ads were paid for by money intended for U.S. Customs and Border Protection, but senior leaders at the agency were cut out of the decision .
A Maryland-based firm, LMD Agency, was awarded a $20 million contract for the new ads, according to public contracting records . The purpose of the contract was listed as a “national media campaign.”
Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have condemned the ads. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called it “propaganda,” while Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring, likened Trump to former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.
“There’s no place for that sort of thing,” Tillis said.
The White House previously defended the ads, calling them “clearly not political” and saying the PSAs were “about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.”
Raquel Coronell Uribe is a politics reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: ‘World Without Cows’ documentary coming to theaters
articles.title_zh: ‘World Without Cows’ documentary coming to theaters
articles.content_orig:
Film explores complex relationship between food, sustainability, biodiversity and people’s livelihoods.
The “World Without Cows” documentary is coming to theaters in the U.S. this October. After a five-year journey to bring this film to life, this is a big moment to experience it on the big screen.
The first showing will be Oct. 9 at the AMC River East 21 in Chicago, Ill., which will be attended by filmmakers Michelle Michael and Brandon Whitworth and executive producer Dr. Mark Lyons. Shows are also scheduled on Oct. 14 at select theatres in Illinois, Wisconsin, Missouri, Iowa, Ohio, Kentucky, Nebraska, Texas, Minnesota, North Dakota and Pennsylvania. Find participating theaters, showtimes, ticket information and more about the theatrical release on the "World Without Cows" website . More theaters are being added daily.
Make a night of it, and bring your crew. Bring your family, friends and colleagues to fill theaters across the U.S. with people ready to rethink the role of cows in the future of our planet. Sold-out showings can lead to a broader theatrical release, and the simple act of you and your network showing up is powerful support of “World Without Cows.”
Related: Packers, imports and profit: “Are you sure about that?”
Cows are tied to some of the biggest questions facing humanity: how we feed a growing population, protect the planet and provide adequate nutrition in communities around the world. Against a backdrop of climate change, food insecurity and rising protein demand, “World Without Cows” challenges what we think we know about cows, climate, health and the future of our planet. Through a global journey spanning 22 countries and five continents, the film explores the complex relationship between food, sustainability, biodiversity and the people whose lives hang in the balance.
Award-winning journalists Michelle Michael and Brandon Whitworth spent five years filming in more than 40 locations, in conversation with farmers, ranchers, scientists and environmental experts. What they found was far from simple: When it comes to cows, it's not black and white.
“The journey showed us that there is no single simple solution to the world’s greatest challenges,” said filmmaker Michelle Michael. “I don’t think the world wants simple answers. It wants a better understanding of how our global food systems work, and that need has never been more urgent than it is right now.”
“Our hope is that ‘World Without Cows’ creates a new baseline for how people engage in hard conversations,” said filmmaker Brandon Whitworth. “The film wasn’t made to be an echo chamber. It was made to bring people together to ask difficult questions about complex issues and be open to different perspectives.”
Related: Meat Institute celebrates 120th anniversary
"Cows have become a symbol in the climate conversation, but the reality is far more complex. By exploring this issue from many angles and in such diverse geographies, the filmmakers give us a much more insightful and hopeful outlook than we might have expected," said executive producer Mark Lyons.
For more information, visit https://worldwithoutcows.com .

articles.title_orig: Child mortality has declined in all world regions
articles.title_zh: Child mortality has declined in all world regions
articles.content_orig:
In 1950, almost one in four children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. In Africa, one in three children died.
The chart shows the change since then. In every region, the mortality rate of children has declined.
In Africa and Oceania, the child mortality rate declined 5-fold, in Asia 10-fold, and in Europe about 27-fold.
Progress was not always steady. The sharp spike in Asia around 1960 was due to the “Great Leap Forward” famine in Mao’s China, the deadliest famine in recorded history.
And the progress is far from finished. The global average has declined to 3.5%, but this still means that about 4.7 million children younger than five years died in 2025 — 13,000 children every single day.
Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century.
In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then.
You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s.
Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it’s still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to.
The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That’s part of the explanation, but far from all of it.
Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much.
Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency — such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances — have played an important role too.
The median age of a country or region is the age that divides its population into two equal parts: half of the people are older, and half are younger. As the population ages, the median age rises.
That’s what this chart tracks. It shows how the median age has changed across world regions from 2000 to 2023, the most recent year for which the UN publishes estimates.
The first thing that stands out is perhaps the least surprising: some regions have much older populations than others. Africa is very young: half of its population is younger than 19. Europe is much older: half of its population is over 42.
But there’s a second point that I think receives less attention in public discussions: how quickly this is changing. Of the six world regions, Latin America is where the median age has increased the most since 2000. It rose by a third, from 23 to 31 years, in a bit less than a generation.
Europe’s population is older, but the median age has been rising more quickly in Latin America this century. That’s largely due to fertility falling later and faster in the latter.
Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada
When people think about global oil, their minds often go toward countries in the Middle East.
But it’s the United States that is the world’s largest oil producer.
The chart shows oil production by country since 1990. As you can see, the US has been the largest producer for the last nine years, since it overtook Saudi Arabia.
Production in the US gradually declined during the 1990s and early 2000s, then increased sharply after 2010 and is now at an all-time high.
This data comes from the Energy Institute’s Statistical Review of World Energy .
In 2025, the amount of foreign aid given by the world’s richest countries fell by almost a quarter . That amounted to a reduction of roughly US$50 billion.
Aid cuts in the United States — and the shutdown of its agency for international development, USAID — got the most attention, and for good reason: the US is the world’s largest aid donor in dollar terms, so its contributions make a huge difference to the global total.
But many other countries cut their aid contributions, too. In the chart, you can see the change among the largest 10 donors (in dollar terms) from 2024 to 2025. This is given as a share of their gross national income.
Contributions fell in eight of the ten countries. Only Sweden and Italy increased their budgets.
The countries shown are the largest donors in dollar terms; some others not shown contribute far more in relative terms: Norway, for example, was the only country to give more than 1% of its national income to foreign aid.
If your job was to sell cars in Turkey in 2022, selling an electric one would be an unusual day at work. Just one new car out of every 100 sales was electric.
By 2025, this had become a fairly normal day. More than one in five new cars were electric — a more than 20-fold increase in just three years. You can see this rapid takeoff in the chart.
Why did electric models become so popular? In 2023, the government introduced tax relief for electric cars, cutting the registration tax compared to petrol and diesel cars. This was timed to coincide with the launch of Turkey’s first domestic electric car manufacturer, Togg , which has quickly become the market leader. Imports of cheaper electric car models, including from China, have also made these markets more diverse and cost-competitive.
This combination of factors has made electric cars far more affordable than they were just a few years ago.
We are all surrounded by nickel. It’s one of the key ingredients in stainless steel, so most of us see it every day: from the pots we cook with, to the pipes in bathrooms, the batteries in mobile phones, and alloys in cars.
For nearly four decades, Indonesia — which has the world’s largest reserves — mined nickel but processed very little of it at home. This changed around a decade ago, when the government banned the export of raw nickel, forcing companies to process it domestically.
That’s the focus of the chart, which shows processed nickel production in tonnes among today’s largest producers.
Indonesia’s production increased more than 60-fold, going from around 22,000 tonnes in 2014 to over 1.4 million tonnes in 2023. The country went from producing 1% of the world’s total processed nickel to 41% in that period.
In 2021, Indonesia overtook China to become the world’s largest producer and is now far ahead. But much of that growth involved Chinese capital. The International Energy Agency reports that Chinese companies now own the vast majority of Indonesia’s nickel refining assets.
