articles.title_orig: Middle East oil exports surpass pre-war levels despite tensions, data shows
articles.title_zh: Middle East oil exports surpass pre-war levels despite tensions, data shows
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil exports from the Middle East have risen above pre-war levels on four of the seven days in the last week of September, provisional data from ship-tracking firm Kpler showed.
However, senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander Ali Fadavi said in a televised interview on Sunday night that only three to four million barrels of oil per day (bpd) are now moving through the route, dismissing the amount as “negligible” when compared with pre-war traffic.
Fadavi said, for the first time, no US vessels were present in the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, the Sea of Oman or even the northern Indian Ocean and US warships are “100 percent vulnerable” to IRGC attacks.
Kpler data showed crude exports from the region exceeded pre-war levels on September 24 and between September 27 and 29, rising to 19.5-22.5 million bpd.
Around that time, Iran claimed success in attacking ships – including US Navy vessels – near the Strait of Hormuz, saying the strikes had forced Washington to move its warships further from the Iranian coast.
Before the US-Israel war on Iran began, exports averaged 18 million bpd between March 2025 and February 2026.
According to Kpler data, the overall tally for crude, oil products, chemicals and non-gas liquids averaged 22.4 million bpd in the seven days to September 30.
On October 1, the seven-day moving average for crude exports was at 18.5 million bpd. This includes transits via the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, exports from terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman.
The number of liquefied natural gas cargoes exiting the Strait of Hormuz also rose in September to its highest monthly level since February.
The figures exclude any vessels that might have crossed the strait with their automatic identification system transponders turned off to avoid detection.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported at least one attack a day in the Strait of Hormuz or in the Gulf of Aden since October 2.
On Sunday, Iran’s top negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the United States accepts Tehran’s seven-day plan to reopen the waterway.

The National Hurricane Center designated a low-pressure area in the southwestern Gulf as Invest 92-L on Monday.
Invest is short for “investigation” and refers to a weather feature that the National Hurricane Center is investigating.
This means we can start getting more spaghetti computer models about this disturbance.
WESH 2 First Warning Weather Meteorologist Cam Tran said the area of interest could become a tropical depression by the end of the week.
The system has 30 mph winds and a minimum central pressure of 1010 mb.
The latest model tracks show a slight easterly shift. However, there is still a big spread in where this could possibly go if it develops.
For now, the system is still expected to remain weak and well west of Central Florida.
Wind shear is forecast to increase across the northern Gulf later in the week. This could prevent anything stronger from developing, keeping the season hurricane-free.

articles.title_orig: Wheat Geneticist Jorge Dubcovsky Named 2026 World Agriculture Prize Laureate
articles.title_zh: Wheat Geneticist Jorge Dubcovsky Named 2026 World Agriculture Prize Laureate
articles.content_orig:
Jorge Dubcovsky, a wheat geneticist at the University of California, Davis, has been named the 2026 World Agriculture Prize Laureate in the category for countries with developed economies.
The award recognizes his contributions to wheat improvement and global food security. It is presented by the Global Confederation of Higher Education Associations for the Agricultural and Life Sciences, known as GCHERA.
Dubcovsky is a distinguished professor in the UC Davis Department of Plant Sciences and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute researcher, according to a press release.
For more than three decades, Dubcovsky’s research has advanced understanding of wheat biology and helped breeding programs apply genomic tools to crop improvement.
His work has identified and characterized genes controlling yield, disease resistance, flowering time, nutrient use efficiency and adaptation to different growing environments. Those discoveries have contributed to improved wheat varieties grown on millions of hectares worldwide.
“The World Agriculture Prize recognizes individuals whose achievements have had a profound and lasting impact on global agriculture and human well-being,” said Doug Steele, chair of the World Agriculture Prize International Committee. “Dubcovsky’s scientific leadership and extraordinary contributions to wheat genetics have strengthened the resilience of one of the world’s most important food crops and have delivered tangible benefits to farmers, food systems and society. His work exemplifies the innovation, excellence, and global impact that the prize seeks to honor.”
Dubcovsky has worked with researchers, breeding institutions, governments and international agricultural organizations to move wheat discoveries into practical use. He has also mentored plant scientists and breeders who continue to contribute to crop research and development.
The World Agriculture Prize recognizes contributions to agriculture and food security through research, innovation, leadership and service. GCHERA also recognizes scientists from countries not classified as having developed economies.
Dubcovsky will be formally honored Oct. 28 at the 2026 World Agriculture Prize Award Ceremony at Nanjing Agricultural University in China.

articles.title_orig: How the Poet Mary Oliver was “Saved by the Beauty of the World”
articles.title_zh: How the Poet Mary Oliver was “Saved by the Beauty of the World”
articles.content_orig:
Filmmaker Sasha Waters wasn’t shy when asked at the National Book Festival about the legacy of her latest documentary subject, the poet Mary Oliver: “I think we’re going to think of her as the (Walt) Whitman of the 20 th century.”
That’s an almost impossible standard, as Whitman became synonymous with the American spirit in the late 19 th century with poems such as “I Hear America Singing,” “Song of Myself,” “O Captain! My Captain!” and “I Sing the Body Electric.” He has since become an iconic American personality of the age, along with the likes of Abraham Lincoln, Mark Twain and Frederick Douglass.
But Oliver, who adored Whitman’s work, won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award for her rapturous odes to nature and our connection to it. She was adored about as much as any poet since Whitman when she died, at 83, in 2019.
She was the nation’s bestselling poet in her late career, quotes from her most famous poems still circulate widely on social media and you can find her work in any bookstore. One of her poems, “Morning at Great Pond,” is featured in the Library’s new exhibit, “ The Declaration’s Promise ,” showcased alongside that of Whitman and a handful of others as representations of the nation’s highest artistic achievements.
And Waters’ new documentary, “ Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World,” is airing on PBS stations across the country as part of its American Masters series. It draws heavily on the Library’s Mary Oliver Papers , a vast collection of some 40,000 items, including her books of poetry, essays and correspondence, plus more than 100 notebooks from her solitary walks in nature.
The documentary also demonstrates how her work is supposed to be heard, with readings by fans such as television host Stephen Colbert, actor Steve Buscemi and actress Helena Bonham Carter.
“Tell me, what is it you plan to do/ with your one wild and precious life?” she asked at the end of one of her most famous poems, “ The Summer Day,” an ode to the joy of just being alive. It comes as close as anything to encapsulating her world view.
She wrote about ponds and sunsets and wild geese and white flowers and dogfish and goldfinches in the field of thistles and hungry bears in the autumn. She wrote in such a way as to make her sense of awe and wonder infectious.
“Joy is not made to be a crumb,” she wrote in “Don’t Hesitate.”
This, from a shy and quiet child.
She was born into what she described as a dysfunctional household during the Depression in a suburb of Cleveland. It was not a place anyone thought of as a paradise of nature. Still, she was drawn to the forests and the ponds and streams, wandering into the nearby woods as a child to escape her unhappy home life. There, she built little huts made of leaves and sticks.
She was interested in poetry early (school, not so much) and while still a teen wrote to the sister of the late poet Edna St. Vincent Millay, asking if she could visit Millay’s house in Austerlitz, New York. Her admiration was such that the sister eventually hired Oliver to help organize the poet’s papers, a project that took years. While in Austerlitz, Oliver met Molly Malone Cook, a staff photographer at The Village Voice, later a gallery and bookstore owner, and always the love of her life.
“Molly was a very strong character, so Molly gave her the belief that she was a great, great talent and was going to succeed in everything,” said John Waters, the avant-garde filmmaker and a longtime friend of the couple (he’s no relation to Sasha Waters), in the documentary.
The pair often struggled to make ends meet — Cook acted as Oliver’s agent, while Oliver taught at a couple of universities — before Oliver’s work began to achieve wide popularity in the 1970s and 1980s. The couple was a fixture in tiny Provincetown, Massachusetts (a summer resort on Cape Cod), for decades.
For a person who never sought out the spotlight and was protective of her privacy, her popularity was a surprising turn and was surprisingly welcomed.
“She was very shy, then blew up to be extremely famous, particularly for a poet, and really sort of enjoyed it,” Sasha Waters said at the festival, in an onstage conversation with book critic Ron Charles.
Oliver wasn’t all that shy and retiring anymore, John Waters, one of the liveliest voices in the documentary, playfully noted. She smoked cigarettes one after another, did not suffer fools gladly and was extremely dedicated to her students. “A Poetry Handbook,” a guide she wrote in the early 1990s, become a staple of the craft.
After Molly died in 2005, Oliver went through a difficult time, including a stint attending Alcoholics Anonymous. Later, on camera, she told journalist Maria Shriver that she had endured sexual abuse as a child and it had made her want to be “invisible” for so much of her life.
It was that sort of unadorned honesty, and bravery, that made her work so relatable to so many for so long.
“She really spoke to people,” John Waters said.

In the Ocean State, aquaculture—the farming and harvesting of primarily oysters, but also clams and quahogs—is a booming business. There are 89 individual aquaculture sites in Rhode Island, covering 392 acres of water, mostly in the state’s salt ponds. Oysters are the No. 1 aquaculture product in the state, with 11 million sold for consumption in 2024. The total value of the state’s aquaculture industry was $7 million.
This three-part series looks into whether pollutants such as PFAS in Narragansett Bay and Rhode Island's salt ponds are impacting shellfisheries and whether these stressors pose a risk to human health from consumption of shellfish . This project examines the economic vulnerability and viability of oyster farmers in light of rising seas, ocean acidification, and coastal development. This series also looks into regulatory blind spots and testing inconsistencies as well as new technology in oyster farming.

Many white dwarfs accrete the debris of disrupted planetary bodies, detected in the form of metal enrichment in their atmospheres, dusty or gaseous circumstellar discs, and photometric transits from debris. The composition of accreted debris has been shown to be diverse yet overall closely resembles Solar System bodies. Here we report the discovery of a white dwarf accreting material that is unlike any Solar System object. The atmosphere of HS 0209+0832 is strongly enriched in trans-iron elements including zinc, copper and niobium but depleted in the canonical rock-forming elements silicon and iron. The composition of the accreted object is consistent with a candidate second-generation planet, formed from the stellar material ejected during the giant phase. The key abundance signature that differentiates it from a first-generation planet is the high enrichment of s-process elements. Photospheric helium and the absence of terrestrial rock-forming elements implies that the white dwarf is accreting from the escaped atmosphere of a photo-evaporating giant planet candidate. This is further supported by the detection of a sinusoidal photometric period of 4.399 ± 0.026 days at an amplitude of 0.120% ± 0.018%, which we attribute to thermal emission phase variability from a planetary day–night cycle or a transiting cometary tail of an evaporating gas giant. The discovery of this second-generation planet that is chemically distinct from first-generation material demonstrates that close-in planets around white dwarfs can form after the main sequence.
HS 0209+0832 is a hot, young white dwarf with an effective temperature of T eff ≈ 35,000 K, a cooling age of t cool ≈ 5 Myr and a hydrogen-dominated atmosphere with an ~1% trace of helium 1 . Such a mixed composition is unusual for a white dwarf of this temperature because helium should sink out of the atmosphere within months 2 , 3 . A far-ultraviolet (FUV) spectrum obtained in 1999 with the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) onboard the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) revealed the presence of carbon, aluminium, silicon, calcium, titanium, nickel and zinc in the atmosphere 4 , as well as ~100 lines that could not be identified. Whereas the presence of helium and metals indicates ongoing accretion, the nature of that external source remained unexplained 4 .
In the 25 years since that study was published, the origin of photospheric metals detected in many other white dwarfs has been unambiguously confirmed as planetary debris 5 , 6 . This motivated a reanalysis of the observations of HS 0209+0832 obtained with HST/STIS, the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE) and the Ultraviolet and Visual Echelle Spectrograph (UVES) mounted on the Very Large Telescope (VLT), along with the broad-band photometry from Pan-STARRS and the Gaia parallax ( Methods ). In a first step, we determined T eff = 35,800 ± 500 K, a surface gravity of log g = 7.90 ± 0.02 and a helium abundance of log(He/H) = −1.90 ± 0.20 (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Extended Data Table 1 ). With these parameters fixed, we computed extensive grids of synthetic white dwarf spectra 7 using detailed lists of metal transitions in the ultraviolet (Extended Data Table 2 ). We matched most of the previously unidentified lines to transitions of copper and niobium, with the latter identified using five Nb III lines and 57 Nb IV lines (Fig. 1 ). We carefully examined archival FUSE 8 spectra of 33 known metal-enriched white dwarfs with temperatures 20,000 K < T eff < 77,000 K and confirm non-detections for niobium within that sample.
The FUSE and HST spectra (both black) of HS 0209+0832 contain many lines of C, Al, Si, Ca, Ti, Ni, Cu, Zn and Nb as well as strong hydrogen and helium lines. The unusual structure of the He II line is not well reproduced by the model, which could be caused by additional absorption from circumstellar gas. We show the model fit used to obtain metal abundances in red.
We measured the photospheric abundances ( Methods ) for nine metals and calculated upper limits on 15 metals (Extended Data Table 3 ). We excluded any lines originating from the interstellar medium in our fit (Extended Data Table 4 ). At the temperature of HS 0209+0832, radiative levitation can support certain elements against gravitational diffusion. We investigated this effect for all detected elements, as well as for N, P and S for which we determined upper limits ( Methods ). We selected these volatiles because they are commonly detected in hot white dwarfs 8 , 9 ; thus, it is unusual they are not observed in HS 0209+0832. We find that, for the measured abundances, radiative levitation is negligible for Ca, S, Ti, Ni, Cu, Zn and Nb. Assuming a steady state between accretion into and diffusion out of the white dwarf atmosphere, we computed the diffusion fluxes for each element. We adopt these mass fluxes as being representative of the material accreting onto HS 0209+0832, as they correct the photospheric abundances for the differential sinking timescales of individual metals (Extended Data Table 3 ). By contrast, the abundances of C, N, Al, Si and P are subject to radiative support. These elements must still have an external origin 10 , 11 , but our analysis cannot determine their mass fractions within the accreting material.
We compare the abundances of the parent body accreting onto HS 0209+0832 to the entire sample of white dwarfs accreting rocky material 12 and to Solar System meteorites 13 , but find no compositional matches (Fig. 2 ). Whereas silicon and iron are two major components of planetary bodies in the inner Solar System, with a combined mass fraction of ~48% in the bulk Earth 14 , we detect only traces of silicon in the atmosphere of HS 0209+0832, compatible with the support provided by radiative levitation, and no iron. By contrast, the material accreting onto HS 0209+0832 is rich in nickel, which shares many geochemical properties with iron, and we measure a nickel-to-iron ratio of Ni/Fe > 2.09, compared with ~0.05 within CI chondrites 15 and the bulk Earth 14 . We find that the trans-iron elements are strongly enhanced relative to calcium compared with solar abundances, particularly niobium, which is over three orders of magnitude more abundant than in the Sun.
We show the number abundances of the metals (Z) in the material accreting onto HS 0209+0832 (red stars) with respect to calcium, normalized to bulk Earth (BE) 74 (solid black line) for all detected metals and metals with strict upper limits. The error bars represent 1 σ uncertainties, and the arrows represent upper limits. The dashed red lines represent the predicted abundance from radiative levitation alone. For comparison, we include the solar abundance pattern 75 (dashed black line), comet Halley 76 (black points) and the abundances of several white dwarfs accreting bulk Earth-like 5 , core-rich 77 , mantle-rich 78 and icy 16 material (green, blue, brown and purple points, respectively).
Most enriched white dwarfs are depleted in volatile elements such as C, N and S, but a minority are volatile enriched, which can be due to accreting either icy bodies 16 or the atmosphere of a giant planet 17 . The only volatile detected in HS 0209+0832 is carbon (Extended Data Fig. 2 ), with a high photospheric abundance that is compatible with fiducial predictions from radiative levitation. However, there are both theoretical and empirical reasons to believe that our fiducial radiative levitation predictions overestimate the importance of this effect. articles.title_orig: How Congo’s Ebola Epidemic Got So Bad So Quickly
articles.title_zh: How Congo’s Ebola Epidemic Got So Bad So Quickly
articles.content_orig:
Bunia, Congo — Congo's Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.
The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday. They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history .
More than 2,000 patients have recovered from the disease, the Reuters news agency notes.
Congo announced an outbreak on May 15 , caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine .
Some health workers gathered in Bunia, the capital of northeastern Ituri province, the heart of the outbreak, to demand payment for owed wages. They were quickly dispersed by officials. The protesting workers included surveillance team members, who identify people exposed to infected patients. They waved placards saying, "No money, no data!" and "No payment for months."
Front-line workers have gone on several strikes since the start of the outbreak to demand payment, further hampering efforts to contain the disease.
An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement.
The worker arrived late Thursday night after being flown to the Netherlands on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement.
"The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country," MSF said.
More than 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus.
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.
A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources.
The attack on Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local official with Congo's ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterward and he died at a hospital of his injuries.
Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation's 17th Ebola outbreak.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country's government for reasons ranging from how it managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.

There are few prizes in cycling more coveted than the rainbow jerseys given to the winners at the various world championships, and two more Elite athletes will get to add to their wardrobes this week at the 2026 UCI Gravel World Championships .
The event will take place in Oct. 10-11 in Nannup, Western Australia, and feature the top performers from the recently concluded 47-event UCI Gravel World Series.
Cycling fans in the United States and Canada will be able to catch every minute of the two Elite races live on FloBikes and the FloSports app, beginning Friday (Oct. 9) at 10 p.m. Eastern, due to the 12-hour time difference.
This discipline is an exciting road-mountain bike hybrid, and it continues to see huge growth at the elite level.
The 2026 Gravel World Championships will be the fifth edition of the event and first held outside of Europe.
More than 50 elite women and over 100 elite men will make their way to Australia to test their skills over a diverse terrain that will include forests, farmland, multiple climbs and, of course, challenging gravel.
More specifically, the courses will feature a mix of dirt, red gravel, hard-packed clay, quartz, mica and pea gravel. The roads wind, climb, switch back and descend through pine plantations, forests and farms.
The climbs of 1-3.5 kilometers at steady gradients are spaced consistently throughout every route, with 13 of the climbs falling between Category 5 and Category 3, and the lower numbers being more difficult.
The Elite riders will be organized based on points won during the UCI Gravel World Series, points at last year’s UCI Gravel World Championships and points from elite competition in other disciplines.
The Elite women will face a 125-kilometer journey Oct. 10, and the men will have their turn in the spotlight over 144 kilometers Oct. 11.
The riders who finish in the top 25% of each competition during the UCI Gravel World Series from October of the previous year through September of the current campaign qualify for the UCI Gravel World Championships. The 2025-2026 Gravel World Series calendar included more than 45 events across 32 countries.
Entrants in the Elite races at the 2026 UCI Gravel Worlds will be representing their home countries.
The winners are considered the world champions and get to wear the rainbow jersey during all competitions of the same discipline during the following season.
But they won’t be the only ones hopping on their bikes down under, as there will be races for riders of all ages and skill levels.
In all, the 2026 UCI Gravel World Championships will feature the two Elite races and 13 gender- and age-based races, though only the Elite races will be broadcast on FloBikes.
For viewers in Canada and the United States, the 2026 UCI Gravel World Championships will be streaming on FloBikes and the FloSports app.
Stage highlights, replays and more breaking news, including recaps and rider interviews, will be on both platforms.

articles.content_orig:
What you need to know: New federal data shows California has surpassed $4.5 trillion in economic production, dominates across sectors, and is a leader in increasing wages and salaries.
SACRAMENTO — While Fox News pundits and politicians in Texas and Florida attack the tentpole of the U.S. economy, Governor Gavin Newsom today announced that California has reached a new milestone as the first U.S. state to surpass $4.5 trillion in economic output. Since 2019, California’s economy has increased by over half, at $1.58 trillion. Recent data also shows that California’s private sector alone has now crossed the $4 trillion mark for the first time.
California didn’t become a $4.5 trillion economy by accident. It happened because working people show up every day and build, grow, manufacture, invent, and move to power this state. Small businesses take the risks. Workers put in the hours. Entrepreneurs bet on the future. That’s the California story, and nobody does it at our scale.
Newly released data from the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis shows that California ranks first in economic output across almost every sector in 2025, including agriculture, manufacturing, technology, entertainment, healthcare, and wholesale trade. California’s economy grew by nearly $300 billion in the past year alone — the largest dollar gain of any state and $76 billion more than second-place taker-state Texas . These gains go deeper than just the GDP — on the individual level, total wages and salaries grew by 5.2%, and California is #1 for personal-income dollar gains this quarter. California also grew faster than Texas, Florida, and New York in 2025, expanding 3.5% after inflation.
California, the nation’s leader in manufacturing , also accounted for over 40% of total U.S. computer and electronics manufacturing and more than half of U.S. film and sound-recording output in 2025. The Golden State, home to 1.2 million manufacturing workers, pays more than $25,000 above the average non-farm wage, supporting families across the state.
The manufacturing jobs multiplier estimates that each manufacturing job supports three more in neighboring communities.
California manufacturers produced $391 billion in economic output in 2025, accounting for 9% of the state’s total GDP.
The state’s manufacturers exported $159 billion in goods in 2024.
Since 2021, California has invested over $215 million in over 675 contracts with employers to train over 194,000 workers in the manufacturing sector.
The Golden State represents only 11.5% of the U.S. population but is responsible for nearly 14% of U.S. GDP, 44% larger than taker-state Texas. California continues to lead the nation economically, outpacing all states and every developed nation , according to a Bloomberg analysis.
The state has more businesses than any other state, including Florida and Texas, supporting strong job creation and expanded economic opportunity for workers across the state. California is also home to more than 4.3 million small businesses , representing 99.8 percent of all businesses in the state and employing 7.6 million people .
As the world’s fourth-largest economy, California continues to lead the nation where it matters most — creating new businesses, attracting venture capital, driving technological innovation, expanding advanced manufacturing, growing high-tech industries, and producing more than any other state. In fact, the Golden State continues to be the #1 state for:
Governor Newsom recently signed new legislation to continue powering California’s economic engine:
✅ Making a major update to California’s antitrust and consumer protection laws. Clamping down on anti-competitive behavior , encouraging competition, and expanding opportunities for entrepreneurs and workers — including by creating new authority for the Attorney General and district attorneys to combat monopolistic behavior while also protecting small businesses.
✅ Helping retailers open and operate faster by allowing businesses undertaking certain tenant improvements to hire qualified architects or engineers to review and certify that building plans comply with life-safety, health, and building code requirements.
✅ Protecting small businesses from abusive financial practices by unscrupulous financing companies.
✅ Ensuring access to small business technical assistance by supporting providers who offer free or low-cost one-on-one, confidential consulting and training. This will help small businesses and entrepreneurs start, grow, expand, and create jobs in California.
✅ Cutting unnecessary red tape that has kept a lower-cost fuel option out of reach for California drivers. Removing a regulatory barrier to authorize the sale of E15 — gasoline blended with up to 15% ethanol — in California.

articles.title_orig: In Photos: British Airways Unveils All-New Airbus A380 Interior With World’s Largest Business Class Cabin
articles.title_zh: In Photos: British Airways Unveils All-New Airbus A380 Interior With World’s Largest Business Class Cabin
articles.content_orig:
British Airways has revealed the completed interior design for its refurbished Airbus A380 , giving the superjumbo the largest business class cabin currently found on a commercial aircraft. The fleet is being transformed from nose to tail, with 106 Club Suites occupying the entire upper deck, alongside new First, World Traveller Plus, and World Traveller cabins on the main deck. British Airways says more than 35,000 individual parts will be installed on each aircraft as part of the extensive refurbishment.
The redesign represents a substantial change in how British Airways intends to use the A380. The existing aircraft will reduce overall capacity while allocating considerably more space to premium cabins. The first completed aircraft is expected to enter service in the coming months, with the refurbishment program continuing across the fleet.
The most visible change is upstairs, where British Airways has replaced its long-standing Club World arrangement with 106 Club Suites spread across the entire upper deck. The carrier previously divided its previous business class seats between the two decks, using the older yin-yang configuration that could leave passengers without direct aisle access. The refurbished aircraft instead uses the airline's established Club Suite concept, with every passenger receiving direct aisle access and a private suite with a closing door. The seat converts into a fully flat bed, while updated storage, finishes, and detailing give the product a refreshed appearance rather than introducing an entirely different seat architecture.
British Airways is also dividing the upper deck into four distinct zones. The arrangement preserves the scale of the A380 cabin while creating smaller areas for passengers and crew to navigate. A redesigned Club Kitchen provides snacks and refreshments between meal services. At 106 seats, the business class cabin is larger than the business sections installed by other A380 operators. Emirates , for example, has as many as 77 business class seats on its A380, although its upper deck also contains First Class and other amenities. British Airways is therefore using the aircraft's unusually large upper deck to create a dedicated premium floor.
The lower deck will carry three cabins, beginning with a new First Class section containing 12 suites. The number is down from the 14 First Class seats on the existing A380, but the redesigned product provides substantially more individual space and privacy. Each First suite has a large enclosed environment, a fully flat bed, a personal wardrobe, and a large 4K entertainment display. The design also introduces an ottoman that allows two passengers traveling together to dine face-to-face. British Airways previously announced the First product as part of its wider effort to establish a new flagship cabin for the airline.
Behind First is an expanded World Traveller Plus cabin with 84 seats. The premium economy section moves entirely to the lower deck and adopts a 2-4-2 arrangement, while the seats receive additional privacy features, larger entertainment screens, and updated storage. The 84-seat cabin represents a significant increase over the 55 World Traveller Plus seats on today's A380.
World Traveller will occupy the remainder of the main deck with 215 seats, compared with 303 in the current configuration. New economy seats include adjustable headrests, larger entertainment screens, and USB-C connectivity, giving the lowest-priced cabin a more modern specification without taking space from the premium products. The result is an aircraft with substantially less economy capacity, while the number of premium seats increases. British Airways is effectively reshaping the A380 around travelers who place a higher value on the onboard experience.
The investment also extends beyond the aircraft itself. At London Heathrow Airport (LHR) Terminal 5, British Airways is developing a new First Wing and First Lounge as part of a broader premium customer experience investment. The new facilities are intended to provide a more seamless journey for premium passengers before they reach the redesigned A380, connecting the airport experience with the upgraded products onboard. First Class passengers will also receive updated dining and bedding, while new amenity kits and refreshed bedding will be introduced elsewhere in the premium cabins. Specially trained First Service Specialists will support the airline's new First dining proposition across its long-haul fleet. Together with the Heathrow investment, those changes show British Airways is approaching the refurbishment as part of a broader premium strategy rather than an isolated aircraft project.
The scale of the work reflects British Airways' decision to retain its A380s rather than simply operate them with their original interiors. The airline's 12 superjumbos entered service beginning in 2013, and their existing Club World product dates from a much earlier generation of business class design. The refurbishment allows the carrier to extend the aircraft's useful commercial life while bringing its onboard products closer to newer British Airways widebodies.
The first refurbished A380 is expected to enter service later this year, although British Airways has not yet published a complete list of routes for the redesigned aircraft. Because the aircraft are being refurbished individually, travelers will need to check the specific aircraft assigned to their flight rather than assuming every A380 service has the new interior. For British Airways, the completed design provides a clearer indication of how the A380 fits into its future fleet. Instead of competing primarily through the number of seats it can carry, the superjumbo will increasingly function as a high-capacity premium platform, supported by upgraded ground facilities at its Heathrow hub. As more aircraft emerge from refurbishment, the critical test will be whether the additional premium inventory and improved airport experience can generate enough revenue to justify keeping one of aviation's largest passenger aircraft in the fleet.

A proposed class-action lawsuit filed Friday in Seattle federal court accuses Starbucks of falsely advertising eight of its protein beverages as “sugar-free” when they actually contain between 13 and 21 grams of naturally occurring sugar per serving.
A proposed class-action lawsuit filed Friday in Seattle federal court accuses Starbucks of falsely advertising eight of its protein beverages as “sugar-free” when they actually contain between 13 and 21 grams of naturally occurring sugar per serving.
The lawsuit claims the Seattle-based coffee giant misled consumers who ordered 20-ounce or 24-ounce “venti” sizes of its new protein-focused drinks. The complaint states that while the beverages may not contain added sugars, the milk used in them introduces lactose, a form of natural sugar, exceeding federal limits for “sugar-free” labeling.
Under federal regulations, beverages labeled as “sugar-free” must contain less than 0.5 grams of sugar per 12-ounce serving.
According to the filing, Starbucks sought to capitalize on consumer health trends, citing market research indicating that 75% of Americans are actively trying to reduce or eliminate sugar from their diets. Plaintiffs also argue that Starbucks violated federal labeling rules by omitting mandatory disclaimers clarifying that the drinks are neither low-calorie options nor designed for weight control.
Venti servings of the beverages contain between 270 and 340 calories, according to the company’s website, which promotes the items as “protein-packed” with “no added sugar.”
Starbucks introduced the line in September 2025 as part of its broader “Back to Starbucks” menu overhaul. The lawsuit targets eight specific items: the Sugar-Free Vanilla Protein Latte, Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Latte, Sugar-Free Vanilla Protein Matcha, Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Matcha, and their iced counterparts.

The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages, citing false advertising and violations of several state consumer protection laws. Representatives for Starbucks and an attorney representing the plaintiffs did not immediately respond to requests for comment today.
False advertising claims regarding sugar content have become increasingly common across the food and beverage industry, with numerous recent lawsuits targeting products marketed as “sugar-free” or “zero sugar” that use substitutes such as allulose.

articles.title_orig: Texas House Agriculture Hearing Lauds New World Screwworm Response, Warns of Mexico Spread
articles.title_zh: Texas House Agriculture Hearing Lauds New World Screwworm Response, Warns of Mexico Spread
articles.content_orig:
Photo by Judy Gallagher via Flickr, CC BY 2.0.
A Texas House Agriculture and Livestock Committee hearing on Friday, October 2 covered a range of topics affecting the state’s agricultural industry, including New World screwworm (NWS) — celebrating the state’s success in stifling its spread and warning about a surge in cases in Mexico.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) lists 52 cases of this flesh-eating livestock pest in the country since the first confirmation in June, 51 of which were found in Texas. One case appeared on the border between Texas and New Mexico, while one is fully within the latter state.
Based on both the USDA’s interactive NWS case dashboard and the Texas Animal Health Commission’s (TAHC) map of NWS zones, the majority of cases are located in West Texas, in counties including Val Verde, Edwards, and Crockett, while a significantly smaller portion is clustered near Roma.
While over a dozen cases occurred in July, August and September saw only four and three cases, respectively. So far in October, only one case has been confirmed — in a dog within Brewster County.
During the hearing, the committee heard testimony from various leaders in the state’s agricultural sector, who discussed a few interim charges assigned by Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows (R-Lubbock) for lawmakers to study ahead of the 90th Legislative Session.
The “invasive species” charge, which encompasses the focus on NWS while also addressing feral hogs and other parasites, reads : “Study the detection and management of invasive species and insects impacting Texas agriculture, including New World screwworm … Examine current prevention, response, and eradication efforts.”
Witnesses generally lauded Texas’ efforts alongside federal partners in preparing for the onslaught of NWS and in its response, while warning that the state is not quite out of the woods, as its neighbor Mexico continues to battle the infestation.
“Tremendous job we did in Texas getting through the summer. No question about it. It surprised the hell out of everybody,” said Thomas Lansford, representing the TAHC.
“But obviously, all hell is breaking loose in Mexico,” Lansford said.
The USDA is currently reporting 45,216 animal NWS cases through September 30 in Mexico, with 2,032 considered active cases.
Another TAHC representative, Dr. Lewis R. “Bud” Dinges, who is the Texas state veterinarian and the executive director of TAHC, similarly lauded the NWS response in Texas, saying, “None of the progress … would have been possible without the vigilance and participation of livestock producers, veterinarians, landowners, and other members of the public.”
But he added, “Our work will continue until the New World Screwworm is pushed out of Texas and back into Mexico. Until the pest is eradicated from Mexico, it will remain a risk to Texas and the United States.”
Since the first case was found in Zavala County in June, the USDA has released over 1.4 billion sterile flies as of October 1 to breed with the pests and prevent reproduction, a method that helped eliminate the NWS from the U.S. in 1966.
This method took center stage during the NWS discussion, as witnesses noted that the continued uptick in the pest’s presence in Mexico meant Texas could not yet rest easy, and that the outbreak would reduce Texas’ protection from the current sterile fly population concentrated in the Lone Star State.
Lansford continued in response to questions from Chairman Ryan Guillen (R-Rio Grande City) about the need for sterile flies to deal with outbreaks in other states: “With flies moving to the north and to the west, and Mexico … New Mexico is already in play … and then that brings Arizona and California into play.”
“If those states have cases, they’re going to take away what sterile flies we continue to disperse over our infested areas, and it's going to diminish what we have at our disposal,” he added.
The hearing concluded with general agreement among witnesses and lawmakers on the panel that while federal and local collaboration on the issue has proved successful, responders must remain vigilant as NWS spreads north and west through Mexico.

articles.title_orig: What impact will climate change have on malaria?
articles.title_zh: What impact will climate change have on malaria?
articles.content_orig:
Climate change could make a number of infectious diseases worse. I expected malaria would be one of them.
That’s concerning, given the huge global burden that it already carries: it kills almost half a million children every year.
But a more complex story emerges from the scientific literature. One where rising temperatures could actually reduce the burden of malaria in some areas, while making it worse in others.
What impact has climate change already had on malaria? Will it make the global fight against it harder or easier in the future?
These are the questions that I want to answer here.
Before we look at how climate change could change the dynamics and distribution of malaria in the future, we need a quick primer on the global burden of the disease today.
This is important because climate change could cause a decline in malaria in some regions, while increasing the prevalence in others. The impact on the overall global burden of malaria will mostly depend on what happens in the worst-affected regions today.
Malaria is an infectious disease present across much of the tropics and subtropics. In the map below, you can see the band of new infections across South America, South and Southeast Asia, and Africa.
The difference between sub-Saharan Africa and other parts of the tropics, though, is huge. Infection rates in sub-Saharan Africa are around 100 times higher than in South America and 50 times higher than in South Asia.
The fact that severe malaria is mostly an African story today is even clearer when we look at where people die from it. More than 95% of the 600,000 people who die from malaria every year live in sub-Saharan Africa. You can see this regional breakdown below. 1
But this chart also makes clear that within sub-Saharan Africa, there are substantial differences in the burden.
Around half of global deaths occur in West Africa — countries like Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, and Liberia. The rest are split between the central and eastern parts of the continent. Southern Africa has extremely low rates of malaria.
This dominance in West Africa is not just about population (we might expect more deaths in denser areas). As you can see in this map of death rates , those living in West Africa are at a much higher risk of dying from malaria.
These are the important background facts to make sense of this article’s focus. Most deaths from malaria occur in sub-Saharan Africa. Within the continent, West Africa is hit the worst. And children are most at risk: tragically, around 70% of malaria deaths are among children. That’s almost half a million children dying of the disease every year.
To understand the link between malaria and climate change, we need to know the basics of the disease’s “perfect conditions”.
Several mosquito species in Africa carry and spread malaria. A dominant one is Anopheles gambiae . It carries and spreads the parasite Plasmodium falciparum , which is what infects humans.
Over many decades, scientists have studied the ideal conditions for these mosquitoes to thrive. The spread of malaria peaks in these species at around 25°C. 2 Transmission drops close to zero below 16°C and above 34°C.
That means the suitability of malaria forms a bell-shaped curve like the one below. It spreads best at 25°C; this suitability drops on either side of it, and eventually becomes negligible.
Temperature is not the only thing that matters. How established malaria already is in a given country or region does, too. As do rainfall patterns: female mosquitoes lay their eggs in standing water, and larvae need water to develop. So, rainfall creates favorable conditions for malaria to spread. There is a limit, though: heavy, persistent rain often washes larvae away, preventing them from developing. An area with moderate rainfall is therefore a good breeding ground for malaria to spread.
Humidity can also have an effect. Adult Anopheles dry out in low-humidity air, so they often live longer in wetter, more humid seasons (and when they live longer, they do a better job of spreading the parasite).
The world has already warmed by around 1.4°C since pre-industrial times. 3
What impact has this already had on the prevalence of malaria?
A recent paper by Colin Carlson and colleagues, published in Nature , estimated the impact of historical climate change on the burden of malaria so far, and projected how this might affect it in the future under different warming scenarios. 4 The paper focused on the burden on children in Africa — as we established earlier, this is the most affected demographic, both in terms of cases and deaths.
They estimate that over the last century — from 1901 to 2014 — climate change has led to a small increase in the prevalence of childhood malaria across sub-Saharan Africa. By “increase”, they mean that rates were slightly higher than they would have been compared to a hypothetical scenario without climate change . The prevalence of malaria has actually declined in recent decades, but for reasons unrelated to climate.
Across the region, this increase was estimated at roughly 1 case per 1,000 children aged 2 to 10. To put this into context, around 24% of children (or 240 in every 1,000) in this region were estimated to carry the malaria parasite at the end of the study period. So, the overall impact has been relatively small and is quite uncertain. 59% of the study’s simulations showed an increase in malaria prevalence, with uncertainty ranging from a reduction of 4 cases per 1,000 to an increase of 6 cases per 1,000.
The bigger impact has been in changing the prevalence of malaria across different parts of the continent. Hotter temperatures might not have led to a large increase, on average, but they have affected its distribution.
Climate change has probably led to a decline in malaria in West Africa, but an increase in the southern and eastern parts of the continent. The following map summarizes this change: you see blue in the West but red, marking an increase, in the East and South.
Remember that West Africa is where the burden of malaria has been, and still is, the highest. A decline there due to climate change has been almost entirely offset by an increase elsewhere on the continent, which is why the effect, on aggregate, is very small.
The chart below shows malaria prevalence in two scenarios: the realistic one the world has lived through, and an alternate reality without human-driven climate change. Malaria has declined in West Africa due to climate change, but has increased in the other three subregions.
To understand why climate change has made things better in West Africa, but worse elsewhere, let’s return to our bell-shaped curve of where malaria thrives.
The study by Carlson and colleagues found results very similar to previous studies on the optimal conditions for malaria-carrying mosquitoes: transmission peaks at around 25°C.
In 1901, the average temperature in West Africa was around 26°C — very close to, but just past, the ideal temperature. 5 Climate change has increased temperatures, pushing them away from the optimum and down the slope.
What has happened elsewhere? East and Central Africa started below the optimum, at around 22°C, and Southern Africa far below, at around 17°C. Higher temperatures in all of these regions have pushed them closer to the optimum. East and Central Africa now sit at around 24°C, and Southern Africa at around 18°C.
It’s this temperature effect that has driven these diverging patterns across sub-Saharan Africa. The authors of the study did not find a discernible signal of climate change in historical drought and flood trends.
What’s crucial is that, while climate change has, on net, probably increased the burden of malaria across sub-Saharan Africa, its impact has been small compared with the many interventions and investments made to control and alleviate malaria. Malaria cases and deaths have not increased, but fallen substantially over the longer term.

articles.title_orig: How to protect your attention in an always-on world
articles.title_zh: How to protect your attention in an always-on world
articles.source: The University of Alabama at Birmingham
articles.content_orig:
Margaret Canter, Ph.D (left) and Maree Jones (right) There was a time when the internet was a briefly visited place. People logged on, did what they needed to do and logged off. That time is gone, and society’s attention now has completely shifted to the online world as digital technology has evolved.
As director of Social Media Strategy at the University of Alabama at Birmingham , Maree Jones has watched the shift happen in real time. Spending 16 years in a field that never stops, Jones has seen technology go from sitting on desks to riding in people’s pockets from the moment they wake up until they go to sleep. Drawing on her years of expertise in an always-online world, Jones provides insight on how to protect attention and focus in the workplace.
The challenge of protecting attention is a workplace concern, and it also is a critical component in mental health and emotional well-being.
Margaret Canter, Ph.D., clinical psychologist and professor of pediatrics in the UAB Marnix E. Heersink School of Medicine and Children’s of Alabama, speaks on the connection between attention and mental health, and shares her insight on attention protection and focus recovery. Canter’s work focuses on providing integrated behavioral healthcare to the pediatric clinic's patient population, which is children from birth through 18, and their families.
According to Canter, attention is a valuable resource because humans can give their attention to only one thing at a time, meaning what individuals choose to focus on and attend to must be worth it.
“When someone is able to focus and sustain their attention, they learn more and can be more efficient in completing their work or tasks,” Canter said. “If we are stressed or anxious about things getting accomplished, we may be preoccupied with those things’ getting done, which would negatively impact our attention.”
Difficulty paying attention and trouble focusing are symptoms of both anxiety and depression. If one already has difficulty paying attention, feelings of anxiety can become heightened, with mood and self-esteem being negatively impacted.
“In the age of social media, productivity isn’t just about how much work gets done. It’s also about how often we’re asked to stop what we’re doing and mentally shift to something else,” Jones said.
Likewise, if someone is already having feelings of anxiety and depression, individuals may not have the motivation to make the effort in their work, tasks and other responsibilities.
Jones says that part of what makes constant connectivity so draining is not the volume of work; it is the volume of decisions. With access to all kinds of information, the mind can be easily susceptible to burnout, and it can be hard to determine which information should be attended to. This persistent hum of pressure can be especially draining for people whose jobs depend on staying informed.
“Burnout has become an increasingly important conversation because we’re finally beginning to understand what long-term exposure to that pace feels like,” Jones said.
Smartphones allow access to all kinds of information at any time and place, including consuming the news via social media instead of traditionally. Because news segments are delivered in 30-second to three-minute intervals, sustaining attention for longer can be more difficult.
“When they’re wanting to read about a news topic or event, I encourage individuals to find one or two sources or individuals they trust and limit their exposure,” Canter said. “If we are intentional about our attention, we will not have the constant stream of information negatively affect our productivity and mood.”
In her role, Jones has the potential to be exposed to thousands of notifications a day. Each one, she says, carries a hidden cost of deciding on what and which information needs to be attended to.
For Jones, she has learned to recognize the warning signs that technology has taken the wheel. The antidote starts with treating attention as a resource worth guarding.
“By the end of the day, people who largely do digital work can feel exhausted because they’ve spent the day managing interruptions and making thousands of tiny decisions,” Jones said.
“Protecting my attention has become just as important to me as managing my calendar, because attention is what allows me to do meaningful work.”
For many people, including Jones, simply spending less time online is not an option. Being online is the job. So instead of avoidance, she recommends building boundaries around intention and learning to let technology work for her, instead of against her.
“I’ve adopted a mindset of being intentional with my time online rather than constantly immersed in it,” Jones said. “Sometimes that means giving yourself permission to mindlessly scroll but setting a timer. Sometimes it means unfollowing accounts that consistently leave you feeling anxious or discouraged.”
Some recommended ways to protect attention include the following:
When people are feeling stressed, they often seek distractions to take their minds off whatever is stressing them. While often associated with unproductivity, distractions can be a tool for attention protection and getting through a tough moment.
“Distraction is an excellent coping skill and one that I often use with children and teens in therapy,” Canter said. “Sometimes we need to get through a tough moment without doing something that would make the situation worse. However, it is important to remember that sometimes you need to come back to whatever is upsetting you and work through it, so it does not cause future problems.”
Having to respond to multiple people, whether digitally or in-person, can be taxing on the mind and attention. To balance responsiveness and attention, Canter encourages having windows of time when they are truly offline. This powerful strategy helps rebuild attention stamina and allows individuals to have higher-quality responses when coming back online.
“As a parent, I try to not have my phone with me during the time I’m helping my kids get ready for bed,” Canter said. “When I’m successful, I’m able to be more present for my kids, which feels good, and we are more efficient in completing the bedtime routine because I am not distracted by whatever it is I’m looking at or whoever I’m talking to on my phone.”
One of the biggest barriers to setting boundaries in terms of responsiveness, Jones says, is the fear of seeming unavailable.
“In workplace culture, we sometimes unintentionally equate responsiveness with value,” Jones said. “Responding quickly doesn’t always mean you’re doing your best work.”
According to Jones, the healthiest teams she has worked with communicate expectations and preferred boundaries clearly. Everyone understands what requires immediate attention and what can reasonably wait. That creates trust without requiring individuals to be constantly interrupted.
“For any communication methods, expectations should be discussed with your manager and your team,” Jones said. “Different jobs require different response times, and having those expectations clearly defined removes a lot of unnecessary stress.”
Digital fatigue is real, and much of it is fueled by the belief that instant communication should always be the norm.
“Just because technology makes instant communication possible doesn’t mean every conversation needs to happen instantly,” Jones said. “Digital work is cognitive work, and sometimes what feels like burnout may actually be decision fatigue.”
Away from work, Jones guards her attention just as carefully, keeping few apps on her phone and even fewer with permission to send notifications.
“Every notification is essentially asking, ‘Can I interrupt what you’re doing?’ Very few apps deserve that permission, especially in my free time,” Jones said. “Just because I work in social media doesn’t mean I have to live in social media.”

articles.title_orig: World Teachers' Day
articles.title_zh: World Teachers' Day
articles.content_orig:
World Teachers’ Day is held annually on 5 October to celebrate all teachers around the globe. It commemorates the anniversary of the adoption of the 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers , which sets benchmarks regarding the rights and responsibilities of teachers, and standards for their initial preparation and further education, recruitment, employment, and teaching and learning conditions. The Recommendation concerning the Status of Higher-Education Teaching Personnel was adopted in 1997 to complement the 1966 Recommendation by covering teaching personnel in higher education. World Teachers’ Day has been celebrated since 1994.
It is a day to celebrate how teachers are transforming education but also to reflect on the support they need to fully deploy their talent and vocation, and to rethink the way ahead for the profession globally.
World Teachers’ Day is co-convened in partnership with the International Labour Organization, UNICEF and Education International.
In 2026, the Day marks the 60th anniversary of the 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers. Six decades on, as the Recommendation is being revised, new challenges have emerged for the profession, from digital technologies and climate change to inclusion, migration and displacement. These pressures affect several dimensions of the status of teachers: their symbolic status, when teaching is not sufficiently recognized or valued; their professional status, shaped by limited autonomy, support or voice in policy-making; and their material status, compromised by salaries, workloads and working environments that do not allow teachers to fully exercise their role.
Under the theme " Standing with teachers: 60 years of protecting the profession, advancing its status and shaping our futures ," the 2026 edition will centre on reviewing the current challenges related to teacher status and the strategies to address them, calling on society and policy-makers to protect, promote and elevate that status.
The global celebration organized at UNESCO Headquarters will feature high-level discussions on protecting and advancing the status of the teaching profession, as well as the award ceremony for the ninth edition of the UNESCO-Hamdan Prize for Teacher Development.
Other celebrations will take place around the world.
Joint Message from Mr Khaled El-Enany, Director-General of UNESCO, Mr Gilbert F. Houngbo, Director-General of the International Labour Organization, Ms Catherine Russell, Executive Director of UNICEF, Mr David Edwards, General Secretary of Education International, on the occasion of World Teachers’ Day 5 October 2026.
"On this World Teachers’ Day, UNESCO, the ILO, UNICEF and Education International call on governments and partners to stand with teachers by advancing the status of the profession  and  ensuring  that  every  teacher,  everywhere,  is  empowered  to  help  build more inclusive, peaceful and sustainable societies."

articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Hits Record as Key Supplier’s Revenue Booms on AI Demand
articles.content_orig:
There's a simple reason the Nasdaq-100 Index closed at new records Friday: The world's biggest company notched its first record since May.
Nvidia , which accounts for 13% of the Nasdaq and 8% of the S&P 500 Index ,  added 1.3% Friday, ending seven weeks of sideways trading surrounding a high-stakes meeting between President Donald Trump and corporate executives leading what Trump calls "super intelligence."
The rally puts the value of Jensen Huang's semiconductor business at just under $5.7 trillion, and based on the price of options trading at Nvidia, it will likely cross the $6 trillion threshold by the end of this month. It should be a comforting notion for equity bulls. Currently, there is about a 50% chance Nvidia will reach a $6 trillion valuation between now and the end of this month, and a 13% chance it happens this week, according to market-maker pricing of deltas on Nvidia options expiring this week and Oct. 30, which measure the sensitivity of options pricing relative to moves in the stock. The odds it happens between now and Dec. 18 is about 67%.
They're also implying about a 1-in-16 chance Nvidia could hit $7 trillion by Nov. 20. Based on the current share count, Nvidia would need to touch $248 to cross the milestone.
"Nvidia's buyback announcement was a bright spot," Ben Emons, managing director at Highline Asset Management, wrote in a note to clients last week. "The buyback is not just a payout but a capital-allocation event that asserts confidence in long-run AI demand."
It's important to note when using deltas to gauge a range of possibilities that the same size move in the opposite direction is also just as likely. While that's largely the case for Nvidia, some of the stock's call options are currently trading with a higher implied volatility than the equivalent puts, Barchart data shows. Such "call skew" is a sign that traders have a bias toward hedging for a rally.

articles.title_orig: Will Powerful Countries Back the UN Chief the World Needs?
articles.title_zh: Will Powerful Countries Back the UN Chief the World Needs?
articles.content_orig:
As the United Nations continues its search for a new leader , Binaifer Nowrojee, president of the nonprofit Open Society Foundations, described the kind of secretary-general that the world wants. But is it the same person that the five permanent members of the Security Council — Britain, China, France, Russia and the US — want, PassBlue asked her.
“We need a secretary-general that is bold, that is not scared to speak truth to power,” Nowrojee told PassBlue on Sept. 24, during an interview that touched on many global issues, including the race to choose the UN’s next top diplomat.
The 15-member Security Council ultimately recommends a candidate to the General Assembly for approval this year, as planned. But the process is currently going through an informal straw-poll phase to assess its candidate of choice.
The latest poll was held by the Council on Sept. 29, after three in July, August and early September, respectively, and like the others before it, the P5, as they are known, have yet to publicly show their hands on who they want to lead the 81-year-old UN. Each P5 has a veto, which can block a substantive Council decision despite majority support and thus end a candidate’s aspirations. A nominee needs to have at least nine votes from the Council and no veto to win the coveted recommendation to the Assembly.
Aglaia Balta, Greece’s permanent representative to the UN and the Council’s monthly rotating president, said on Oct. 1 that members would be consulted on using color-coded ballots in the next two straw polls, slated for midmonth and end of the month. The color ballots distinguish the P5’s votes from those of the 10 elected members, revealing whether a candidate faces opposition from a permanent member without identifying which country cast the no vote.
The candidates, now numbering seven, after Michelle Bachelet of Chile dropped out on Sept. 20, have been straddling a tightrope in their respective campaigns, avoiding statements that could put them at crossroads with the P5. Despite the balancing act, some P5 have publicly signaled reservations about candidates. Bachelet, Chile’s two-time president, announced her withdrawal after poor results in the first three informal ballots.
Opposition from Washington was a hurdle she could not surmount because of her perceived pro-abortion stance and other matters. (Relevant US officials, for starters, never met with her, according to a diplomat familiar with her campaign.) China has said it would prefer a woman secretary-general. That could complicate the bids of candidates like Rafael Grossi of Argentina, Macky Sall of Senegal and Olara Otunnu of Uganda. Grossi also faces a potential block from Russia, which has reportedly suggested it may oppose candidates with European Union or NATO citizenship.
Besides being Argentine, Grossi holds Italian citizenship. Maria Fernanda Espinosa, a candidate who is a former vice president of Ecuador and is backed by Antigua and Barbuda, has Spanish citizenship. So far, Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica and Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett have led the informal polls, but neither has emerged as an obvious consensus choice for the Council to recommend to the General Assembly. Color-coded ballots will better reveal their chances.
The interview has been edited for clarity and condensed for brevity. Some questions have been reordered for better flow.
PassBlue: Given the UN’s financial crisis, political tensions and struggles to resolve conflicts and fund development work, would a woman secretary-general step onto a glass cliff?
Binaifer: The United Nations has carried us well for the last 80-plus years, and there’s been great steps forward on a variety of issues through the UN and a rules-based world order, and people still want that. Governments still want that, but we are now at a point where the world is different. When the UN was set up, it was four or five empires that actually set it up and have presided over it. So there are inequalities and privileges that were built in that no longer fit today’s world.
Today, we don’t have a world of four or five empires. We have a world of 193 countries that sit and want a place at the table. Demographics are different. Eighty-five percent of the world’s population is now sitting in the global majority, only 15 percent in Europe and the United States. The UN has reached the end of how it can function in the way it’s functioned, and a reset is required, and that is the case for any organization.
The most important thing we need right now is a secretary-general who is visionary and bold and is ready to take this organization into the future. As the first woman to lead the Open Society Foundations, it is incredible to me that over 80 years, not a single woman has served as the UN secretary-general.
It is symbolic of the types of exclusions that have limited the abilities of the UN, even as it has espoused equality, even as it espoused human rights principles; it’s an important thing that it walks the talk internally of what it needs to do. We need a secretary-general who will lead us into the future that this next generation is going to live in.
PassBlue: What does the world need from the next secretary-general that might conflict with the P5’s priorities?
Binaifer: We need a secretary-general that is not scared to speak truth to power, that substantively can identify the key issues we need to focus on in this next century and is not scared to make some of the hard decisions that will require. We also need a secretary-general that is a bridge builder. They still have to work with member states. They still have to build coalitions around the agendas. But let’s not have a secretary- general that relinquishes the entire reform agenda and limits it only to budgets and headcounts. We have a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to press a reset button. Let’s do it properly.
PassBlue: How do you see African countries engaging in multilateral, bilateral and trilateral AI discussions and using the technology?
Binaifer: First of all, we know Africa is the youngest continent, and every one of those young people has a phone in their hand, so we know that there’s a lot of familiarity and that young Africans are leaning into technology. They’ll lean into artificial intelligence. They may not be the architects of the structure, but they will be the users, and they will innovate and find ways to have this integrated into their lives.
What we want to ensure is that the harms that we are seeing in places where children or hate speech, those kinds of things, that African governments take steps to put in a regulatory environment, because now we know those lessons. We see Australia stopping social media for children under 16. We know that women politicians, for example, get much more hate and abuse online compared to male politicians. So African governments can actually make policy decisions to limit the harms but also benefit, to have their young people benefit from the good possibilities that that technology and artificial intelligence will bring.
PassBlue: How can African countries move beyond consuming technology to creating economic benefits for young people and for their national economies?
Binaifer: There’s huge innovation in Africa on many levels. Take a place like Kenya, where technology for money transfers with M-Pesa happened long before other countries were doing it, and you find very savvy tech people in Gen Z organizing protests on social media to call on the government to do things about their issues. We also see innovation in organizations like Gearbox in Kenya or others, and the difference between the US and Africa in terms of why does innovation actually appear in the US in the tech space. Because the US government has invested in providing funds for innovation.

articles.title_orig: Disease ecologist on the emergence of the new world screwworm and how to stop it
articles.title_zh: Disease ecologist on the emergence of the new world screwworm and how to stop it
articles.content_orig:
As a new parasite with flesh-eating larvae threatens the nation's livestock industry, a team of Virginia Tech researchers will be on the frontlines of defense.
Led by Luis Escobar, an associate professor of fish and wildlife conservation, the team is working on one of 40 breakthrough projects funded through the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to develop an integrated preparedness and response system against the re-emergence of the new world screwworm in the Americas.
“Preventing a screwworm invasion protects food production, food prices, rural economies, family farms, wildlife populations, companion animals such as dogs and horses, and public health because the screwworms can also affect people,” said Escobar.
Earlier this summer, the USDA confirmed that the new world screwworm fly reached south Texas, threatening the livestock industry for the first time in decades.
Screwworm-related losses exceeded $200 million annually in the 1950s, the equivalent of roughly $1.8 billion today, before eradication efforts succeeded.
According to Escobar, mitigation measures include mandatory physical inspections and anti-parasitic treatments for cattle at southern border ports, as well as stricter movement requirements for animals entering Texas.
As part of the project, Virginia Tech will expand collaborations with Texas A&M, North Carolina State University, the University of Kansas in the United States, Universidad de San Carlos, and Universidad del Valle in Guatemala.
“Rather than addressing one aspect of screwworm control, this project creates a complete decision-support framework that connects surveillance, genetics, producer behavior, and predictive modeling,” Escobar said.
Luis Escobar is an associate professor in the College of Natural Resources and Environment at Virginia Tech. He is a member of the Pandemic Prediction and Prevention Destination Area, the Invasive Species Collaborative, and the Fralin Life Sciences Institute’s Center for Zoonotic and Arthropod- borne Pathogens and Global Change Center.
His research focuses on biogeography, ecology, and evolution of infectious diseases across landscapes.
To schedule an interview with Escobar about the new world screwworm, its reemergence, and how to stop the parasite from threatening food systems and agriculture, email mediarelations@vt.edu .

That match will take place on finals day at the Players Championship Finals in Minehead â an event Littler has also yet to qualify for having skipped the majority of Pro Tour events this season.
He is currently ranked 126th in the Players Championship order of merit and only the top 64 qualify.
Four Players Championship events remain, but two of those are in Den Bosch in the Netherlands - where Littler withdrew from events recently after being subjected to boos by the crowds .
Littler has won successive full World Championships and won the youth title as a 16-year-old in 2023, but the semi-final loss to 23-year-old Crabtree was his second successive exit at that stage having lost to Beau Greaves in 2025. He could though enter four more times, with the tournament open to players aged 23 or under at the start of the season.
The loss is the latest in a series of surprise exits for Littler, who was knocked out of the World Grand Prix in the first round by Luke Woodhouse and lost to Jonny Clayton in the quarter-finals of the World Series of Darts finals.

That’s a nicer name than ‘stalker mode.’
Instagram is internally developing a possible new feature that seems tailor-made to allow for nefarious behavior. Leaker and reverse engineer Alessando Paluzzi posted on X with the discovery of an Instagram feature billed as "read-only mode." According to the uncovered screenshots, this option allows for a session where "you can't like, comment, message, follow or view stories" on the social network, which would allow a user to browse the platform without leaving any type of paper trail about what they were viewing. It appears to be a concept for Instagram Plus accounts from the images shared.

A spokesperson from Instagram told Engadget that read-only mode "is an internal only exploration, not testing externally at all." So this feature is far from launching if it ever does, and tech platforms will regularly try out features that never see the light of day for users. But it also doesn't suggest whether there's any acknowledgement internally that this type of reduced visibility could be used for stalking or other criminal purposes.
