articles.title_orig: Operations research program prepares students to solve real-world challenges
articles.title_zh: Operations research program prepares students to solve real-world challenges
articles.content_orig:
The following story originally appeared on the website for the William & Mary College of Arts & Sciences. – Ed.
“When they say, ‘Houston, we have a problem’ in movies, they are hailing mission control. However, when mission control has problems, they contact us,” said Elisa Leal Acevedo M.S. ’25, an engineer in NASA’s Mission Evaluation Room (MER) during the Artemis II mission.
The MER monitors all data coming in from the Orion spacecraft, searching for anomalies. Acevedo, who graduated from William & Mary with a master’s degree in computational operations research, utilized her operations skills to assist the Artemis II mission earlier this year.
The Computational and Applied Mathematics master’s degree with a Concentration in Operations Research (CAM-COR) is an updated name for a long-standing program at W&M. The new program, which took effect in August 2026, is also offered as a Bachelor’s-to-Master’s Accelerated Pathway (BMAP) for W&M undergraduates.
The core of the program consists of courses in operations research, mathematical modeling for random processes, probability and optimization. These theories are correlated to real-world business and safety challenges, such as optimal traffic light timing and customer queuing.
The program is led by seven distinguished professors, who come from a range of backgrounds that inform their respective classes and research, helping students connect mathematical modeling with real-world decision-making.
Graduates apply their degree in an array of fields. Recent CAM-COR graduate Acevedo worked six shifts in NASA’s MER in Houston for the Artemis II mission this past year. In her role as a subject matter expert on the Flight Software Console team, Acevedo monitored Orion’s Environmental Control and Life Support Subsystem’s software, making sure it was operating as expected in real time.
“My COR degree helped me apply the decision-making skills I developed in the program when encountering anomalies in the MER,” Acevedo said. These skills allowed her to quickly assess courses of action, analyze probability of recurrence and perform risk analysis. She also optimized limited spacecraft resources such as bandwidth allocations, considering operational constraints at the same time.
“Post-mission, I am now exploring software reliability methods that can be applied to the flight software on future missions,” she said.
While Acevedo’s work focuses on the depths of space, a current student is specializing in defense research. Anne Kredell ‘26 first took CAM-COR classes as an undergraduate at W&M and is now a master’s student in the program. She applied her studies this past summer as an intern for the Naval Information Warfare Center in San Diego, where she focused on radio frequency machine learning.
Though this was a new area for Kredell, she was able to adapt and tackle the project. “My COR coursework prepared me to approach this challenge, and my mathematical skills allowed me to suceed,” Kredell said. “The technical skills and critical-thinking abilities I developed in those classes were integral to my success this past summer.”
Faculty in the program put the versatility of a CAM-COR degree on display through their diverse professional and research experiences, showcasing the breadth of opportunities the degree can support. For example, adjunct professor Dave Williams is a former chief operating officer of the U.S. Postal Service, while Rex Kincaid, Chancellor Professor of Mathematics, is conducting research in the marine science world. Kincaid is developing optimization models to determine the best locations to build new oyster reefs in the Chesapeake Bay.
Even closer to campus than the Chesapeake Bay, Larry Leemis, a professor for the COR program since 1993, conducts research for Colonial Williamsburg. In the 1990s, he worked to determine the optimal number of weekly tourist guides to print. Three decades later, Leemis is researching new topics for the Colonial Williamsburg Foundation, such as optimizing maintenance routines for equipment.
These professors, through studying a range of applications of operations research, utilize their experience to encourage students to find the next problem that can be solved with mathematical modeling.
After a fruitful internship, Kredell is eager to continue working in operations research, specifically within the defense sector, post-graduation. “This degree prepares me for a wide array of careers,” she said. “Beyond the specific technical tools I am learning, the program is teaching me how to approach varying problems systemically and how to communicate my findings clearly.”
From Chesapeake Bay oyster health to NASA lunar missions, the CAM-COR master’s degree program continues its legacy of instilling real-world problem-solving skills, preparing students to optimize systems across industries.
Applications for spring admission to the program are open until Oct. 15 .
Rebecca Ries '27, College of Arts & Sciences

articles.title_orig: Sam Altman says the world should accept some ‘bad things’ happening with AI as the industry signs on to Trump’s voluntary safety pact
articles.title_zh: Sam Altman says the world should accept some ‘bad things’ happening with AI as the industry signs on to Trump’s voluntary safety pact
articles.content_orig:
Following a controversy-filled summer in which OpenAI’s models executed more than one unauthorized hack, CEO Sam Altman said the world should accept some “bad things” happening with AI for the sake of all the good the technology will bring.
During Politico’s Decoded podcast , he was asked where his and OpenAI’s view of new AI rules differed from that of Anthropic and its CEO, Dario Amodei.
“We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” Altman replied.
The comments come as debate intensifies over how much regulation and what safeguards should be applied to AI while Congress has yet to pass a law dealing with the technology. Fears over the tech recently increased after an Anthropic researcher resigned last month and warned AI companies are “ gambling with our lives ” by rushing AI development toward potentially self-improving systems that could threaten humanity.
Anthropic has advocated for AI regulation, and Amodei last month called for a global slowdown in AI development to address the tech’s risks. Altman and other AI executives agreed with him on slowing down .
In August, OpenAI also backed a California law requiring AI companies to publish a public safety framework and a plan for mitigating catastrophic risks, as well as to report any loss of control of an AI model. It even asked for that law to go beyond reporting to include monitoring of AI models during their development.
OpenAI president Greg Brockman also joined other AI executives in signing an agreement at the White House last week to establish voluntary standards for the industry.
Still, that falls short of calls for tougher regulation coming from other AI leaders like Amodei, who has proposed an FAA-style regulator that could require testing and auditing of AI models or block or reverse their release if they don’t meet the bar for public safety.
In the interview with Politico, Altman said it would be impossible to avoid every bad thing that AI could be used for. The alternative would be to severely restrict access to the technology, which he said would be unacceptable.
“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, like, we’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no kind of, like, misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen, because I think people will do tremendously, orders of magnitude, more good stuff than bad stuff,” he added.
Altman said AI companies should tread carefully, though, and draw a line when it comes to “catastrophic risks,” which have recently taken on renewed significance given recent hacks by AI models on third parties.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment.
Concerns over the possibility of AI escaping human control have recently accelerated following hacks executed by OpenAI’s models on open-source AI platform Hugging Face and the Australian government . Anthropic last month also said it had discovered four incidents in which its AI models had gained unauthorized access to third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations.
While much of the AI safety debate has centered on losing control of AI, Altman said restricting access to AI too severely in the name of safety could be harmful too.
“That also is a way that this can go horribly wrong because people are shut out of the kind of power and benefits and control and agency over the future they should have,” he added.
The CEO said AI developers should strike a middle ground instead.
“Accept bounded risks, accept risks that we understand in exchange for the benefits, and liberty, agency, all those things,” he said. “But don’t accept, like, the really catastrophic risk.”

articles.title_orig: Arizona cookbook author explores the spicy world of salsa — and its importance to Sonoran food
articles.title_zh: Arizona cookbook author explores the spicy world of salsa — and its importance to Sonoran food
articles.content_orig:
LAUREN GILGER: Red or green? That might be the most important question ever asked in Sonoran cuisine. But, when it comes to salsa, our next guest this morning says it’s just the beginning.
Jackie Alpers is a Tucson-based cookbook author and food photographer and Sonoran cuisine expert, and she just came out with a free digital salsa cookbook outlining her essential salsa recipes, ingredients and more.
And she’s on the line now to tell us more.
LAUREN GILGER: Good morning, Jackie.
JACKIE ALPERS : Good morning!
LAUREN GILGER : OK, so salsa just means sauce in Spanish? This blew my mind.
JACKIE ALPERS : I know! So, technically, all sauces are salsas, and vice versa, I suppose.
LAUREN GILGER : That’s great. So, that I mean, basically means that you’ve got a huge variety and diversity of things that can be called salsas. Give us a sense of just everything that’s in here, right? We’ve got not just, you know, green salsas or red salsas, but so much more.
JACKIE ALPERS : Right, we have a rainbow of salsas because there’s there’s wonderful salsas that are every hue, from yellow to black, and, of course, red and green. But there’s also — one of my favorite dark salsa, dark, heavily covered salsas and moles. I’ve got, and I guess salsas are usually thought of often as dips, and so I’ve got my chunky guacamole recipe in there. I’ve got my Amarillo, my Amarillo yellow salsa, which is a habanero-based mustardy salsa, is thick, so it could also be used as as a dip for chips. Yeah, but I’ve got pico de gallo, which is like multicolored technically.
LAUREN GILGER : One of my favorites, for sure. So, I mean, Jackie, tell us about your own kind of journey in in salsa. I mean, you’ve been writing about and learning about Sonoran cuisine for a very long time now, but it sounds like you learned how to make salsa from from some of the best there in Tucson.
JACKIE ALPERS : I have. You know, I was I’m been fortunate enough to have learned from the best. I started working at El Charro Café, which is the oldest family-owned Mexican restaurant in the United States, in the early '90s. Ah, one of my favorites still. And they the family kind of took me under their wing, and I worked in the kitchen, I worked as a bartender, and I worked kind of doing, in the the job where you make the plates look all pretty, which is expediting, I think it’s called.
And so I spent a lot of time in the kitchen with the with the family and with their chefs, and I really learned the the kind of backbone of what makes Sonoran cuisine what it is from them. And Carlotta Flores, in particular, is such a historian, and she really does an amazing job of of teaching people about Sonoran cuisine, and I’ve benefited greatly from that over the years.
LAUREN GILGER : All right, so salsa, such a cornerstone as you’re describing there of Sonoran cuisine. And the roots of it are are kind of as diverse as the region, right? Like, you write that the roots of salsa can be traced back to Native American, Spanish, Mexican history, right? U.S. occupation, too.
JACKIE ALPERS : Yes! There’s there are salsa recipes that go back, you know, five or more generations that are still being made today, family recipes that have been passed down. There’s so many different influences, and everybody has put their spin on it, which is one of the things that makes Sonoran cuisine so special in general, is that there are these unique influences that come from all over the place.
LAUREN GILGER : Yeah. I want to talk about, before we let you go here then, a couple of these recipes, right? I mean, you you kind of outline very nicely you’ve got like pantry essentials that can be useful for folks that you probably have in your house or could have in your house, and then sort of the fresh ingredients.
I want to ask about chilies, though, because that’s got to be pretty essential to making a lot of salsas. They can be dried or fresh. What are some of your favorites?
JACKIE ALPERS : Oh, my gosh! Well, I think my all-time favorite chili is the chiltepin, which is which is, it’s called the mother of all chilies, and it grows wild here in the Sonoran Desert. And they’re tiny, little pea-sized chilies. On the Scoville scale, they’re very, very hot, but since they’re so small, if you crumble them, they’re usually served dried, but they also serve them pickled. I prefer them dried and crumbled, like you would red chili flakes into anything. And they’ve got a different flavor profile than, say, your typical red chili flake and that they’ve got a brightness, they’re almost citrusy, they’re a little bit sweet. And they really do add a really distinct flavor in a way that other chilies do not. And in some I mean, they’re even they’re so special because they’re kind of our chili, you know, like
LAUREN GILGER : Yeah, to this region. Hatch chili season is about now or coming up, right? Any favorites that use Hatch chilies in these salsa recipes?
JACKIE ALPERS : Oh, yes! Well, OK, I think that as far as green chilies go, that there’s like the Anaheim chili that people around the rest of the country can’t always find Hatch chilies, but here, any pico salsa, which is the chunky green chili salsa, is great with those Hatch chilies. You can make a fantastic like like a creamy ranch with just blending a Hatch chili in there with your ranch and drizzling. I love it on like pizza. But and I think I for like I mean, even salsa verde, which can use those Hatch green chilies, but I kind of prefer serranos because they’re a little spicier.
But really, if you want a a slightly milder chili than, say, a jalapeño, and of course Hatch chilies vary in heat greatly, but if you want you can pick up a and they’re usually marked as like spicy to not spicy in the supermarket, the Hatch. So, if you pick up the milder Hatch chilies, you can sub that out for other chilies when you want something a little less spicy.
LAUREN GILGER : Yeah. OK, so last minute here, Jackie. You outlined all of the various types of salsas involved here, from enchilada sauces to moles, you have a BBQ hot wing salsa here. Do you have a favorite? What’s your go-to?
JACKIE ALPERS : My go-to is the chiltepin salsa, which is a fresh, blended salsa. You can make it in five minutes. All you need just like a tablespoon of chiltepins with like a can of tomatoes, it’s like so easy to make, and a garlic purée, an onion, and you don’t, it doesn’t, it’s not cooked at all, so it’s got that fresh brightness and the chiltepin, ah, it’s my all-time favorite.
LAUREN GILGER : So, on the red or green question, you’re on the red side?
JACKIE ALPERS : Well, no. I mean, it depends. I mean, like I love it depends on the red or green, because they vary so much. But like on breakfast burritos, for whatever reason, I tend to go like the tomatillo green. OK, OK. But for dipping, I don’t know, I love I love them all. I can’t say.
LAUREN GILGER : It’s like choosing a favorite child. OK, I won’t ask. Exactly. All right, that’s Jackie Alpers, a Tucson-based cookbook author, food photographer joining us to talk about salsas. Jackie, thank you so much for coming back back on. Appreciate it.
JACKIE ALPERS : Sure. Thanks so much for having me, Lauren.

articles.title_zh: Chiang Mai conference opens to explore “Being Church in the World Today”
articles.content_orig:
A gathering of World Council of Churches (WCC) commissions and reference groups on Life, Justice and Peace opened in Chiang Mai, where ecumenical leaders will explore what “ Being Church in the World Today” means.
Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay, general secretary of the World Council of Churches adressed the Joint Conference of WCC Commissions and Reference Groups on Life, Justice and Peace on the openning day of the conference in Chiang Mai, Thailand, 5 October 2026.
WCC general secretary Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay, in his opening address, offered a WCC perspective on ecclesiology, mission, witness, and hope.
“ Humanity faces wars and armed conflicts, growing inequalities, displacement and migration, ecological destruction, technological disruption, artificial intelligence, religious and political polarization, declining confidence in institutions, and profound questions concerning human dignity and the future of life itself,” he said. “ At the same time, Christianity itself is experiencing major transformations.”
The church is God's before it is ours, reflected Pillay. “ Here unity is not an ecclesial luxury,” he said. “ It is related directly to Christian witness.”
He further noted that a divided church struggles to proclaim a reconciled Christ. “ This is particularly important for the ecumenical movement,” he said. “ The WCC ’ s understanding of unity cannot be reduced to organizational uniformity.”
Dr Prawate Khid-arn, assistant general secretary for ecumenical relations of the Church of Christ in Thailand, prayed that the meeting will renew people ’ s hearts, deepen their commitment, and give them fresh energy and courage for the journey ahead.
“ May our discussions lead not only to words and recommendations, but also to meaningful actions that bring hope to those who suffer, restore human dignity, strengthen justice, care for God's creation, and contribute to genuine and lasting peace,” said Khid-arn. “ May the Holy Spirit guide your conversations, inspire your discernment, and strengthen our common witness.”
Rev. Grace Moon, general secretary of Christian Conference of Asia, noted the context of the meeting in Asia—a region full of spiritual richness, cultural diversity, and resilience, yet also a place where many still face challenges like inequality, displacement, violence, discrimination, and climate change.
“ Our Christian faith means we cannot ignore suffering or injustice—we are called to stand with those who are hurting, excluded, or silenced,” said Moon. “ We cannot solve these problems alone.”
Moon further noted that climate injustice, conflict, and discrimination are all connected. “ Our calling goes beyond charity—it is about working together for justice, healing, and the well-being of all people and creation,” said Moon.
The conference marks the second time that WCC commissions related to the Life, Justice, and Peace programme are meeting - the first such gathering was held in Geneva in 2024.
The first day of the conference currently underway began with pilgrimage encounters, giving participants an opportunity to meet local communities and organizations in and around Chiang Mai working on issues including clean air, migration, HIV and health justice, and interfaith dialogue.

articles.title_orig: Goddard School Preschoolers Experience Broadcast Journalism for World News Day
articles.title_zh: Goddard School Preschoolers Experience Broadcast Journalism for World News Day
articles.content_orig:
Preschoolers at The Goddard School in Plymouth recently got a hands-on introduction to broadcast journalism during a special visit from CCX News anchor Emily Haugen in honor of World News Day.
During the visit, the young students stepped behind the anchor desk, practiced using real microphones and tried their hand at interviewing. The interactive session gave them a taste of how news reporting works, featuring lighthearted conversations about their favorite colors, sports and pets at home.
“So I just asked all of them what their favorite color is, so I’ll ask that to you, too,” Haugen asked one student during a practice interview. “What is your favorite color?”
“Purple!” the student replied.
“Why is purple your favorite color?”
The activity aligns directly with the school’s focus on inquiry-based learning, according to school owner Anthony Miller.
“I think any time you can add curiosity to anything, kids learn well with that,” Miller said.
The Goddard School frequently hosts visitors from various professional backgrounds to introduce students to different career paths and foster early curiosity about the world around them.

articles.content_orig:

Posted on October 5, 2026 in News
Dear Brothers and Sisters in Christ,
On October 18, we celebrate World Mission Sunday, a powerful reminder of our shared responsibility to proclaim the Gospel to all nations. It is a day when Catholics around the world unite in prayer and solidarity to support the missionary work of the Church.
We are all called to be a part of this mission work. In his last words before ascending to heaven, Jesus told us, “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” (Mt 28:19), and for 2,000 years the Church has been at work in this task. And we are far from finished! Two-thirds of the people alive — 5.5 out of 8.1 billion — still have no relationship with Christ or his Church. Bringing people to Jesus is the work of the Church, and all of us together have a part to play. Today, we have a singular means to do so: World Mission Sunday.
The second collection we take up on World Mission Sunday helps extend the Church’s missionary work to places where the Church barely exists, where the Gospel has never been heard before, and where the Church is too young, too persecuted, or too poor to sustain herself.
On World Mission Sunday, we stand in solidarity with the missionaries, priests, religious sisters and brothers, and lay leaders serving in the 1,130 mission dioceses — spanning Asia, Africa, Latin America, Oceania, and the Middle East — that depend on our prayers and financial support to continue proclaiming Christ and building His Church.
The year’s World Mission Sunday celebration is unlike any other in our lifetime for two reasons.
First, this World Mission Sunday marks the 100th anniversary of its establishment by Pope Pius XI in 1926. This centenary is an opportunity to mark it with renewed missionary zeal. This year’s theme, “One in Christ, United in Mission,” chosen by Pope Leo XIV, invites us to rediscover the profound unity we share in Christ through baptism and how our baptismal identity overflows into the mission to bring others into communion with God and us.
Secondly, the beatification of Archbishop Fulton Sheen on September 24 reminds us of the importance of the missions. While many know him best for his TV presence, books, and charismatic eloquence, he repeatedly said, “My greatest love has always been for the missions of the Church.” For 16 years, as National Director of The Pontifical Mission Societies in the United States, he poured his talents into World Mission Sunday and distributed the proceeds diligently to the missions. We can surely count on his intercession for World Mission Sunday 2026.
Pope Leo XIV recognizes how important World Mission Sunday is for the Church. He spent a large part of his priestly ministry as a missionary in Peru, serving communities in the Andean highlands and rural villages, and has noted how dependent he was on the support of the Church universal through World Mission Sunday.
Last year, he became the first pope in history to record a short video that could be played before Mass, in which he appealed, “Please help me help missionaries everywhere.” That’s what World Mission Sunday does: to help Pope Leo care for the 1,130 missionary dioceses and territories under his supervision through the Dicastery for Evangelization.
Please respond to his appeal as generously as you can. Visit pontificalmissions.org/wms-2026 for full details.
I am praying that World Mission Sunday will be a blessing for our diocese and help foster increased zeal for the missions within all of us. Let us pray together that the Holy Spirit will renew in us the fire of the early Church, that we might truly be One in Christ, United in Mission, and that we will grow in missionary awareness, solidarity, and responsibility.
In Hope, united in Christ’s mission,
Most Rev. James V. Johnston, Jr. Bishop of Kansas City-St. Joseph

articles.title_zh: SoCal heat wave shatters multiple records, and the misery is far from over
articles.content_orig:

Southern California has seen some toasty Octobers, but this year’s start to the fall season has been marked by a persistent heat wave that’s shattered records and ushered in an unprecedented streak of 100-degree days.
The extreme heat is driven by a persistent high pressure ridge that has parked over the region causing sinking warming air with very little overnight relief. That is paired with down-sloping winds and uncharacteristically warm ocean temperatures — driven in part by an El Niño that has reduced Southern California’s sea breeze, frequently known as its natural air conditioning.
“We’re going on Day 4 of this really significant heat wave and we still have several more days of heat,” said Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Oxnard. “We do have heat events in October, but this streak of 100-plus days is definitely starting to become pretty notable.”
The average number of 100-degree days in downtown Los Angeles in a typical October has been closer to zero than one since the weather service began keeping records in the late 1800s. This month, downtown is on a four-day consecutive streak of temperatures 100 degrees or higher — the longest consecutive stretch in October since records began.
Downtown is currently tied for the most 100-degree-plus days in October with 1958 and 1971, but could surpass those years if the mercury hits 100 degrees Tuesday, according to the weather service.
“If we get another one tomorrow, then we would be at the most 100-degree-plus days in October in downtown L.A. ever,” Schoenfeld said.
Saturday’s game started 45 minutes after the National Weather Service issued an extreme heat warning as the temperature reached 100 degrees at first pitch at Dodger Stadium.
The current heat wave already has broken daily heat records across the Southland.
Downtown Los Angeles broke a daily heat record Monday with the mercury reaching 104 degrees, shattering the previous record of 101 set in 1954 and tied in 1971.
The Burbank Airport hit 101 degrees Sunday, breaking the previous record of 100 set in 1964. Camarillo hit 99 degrees, inching past the previous record of 98 set in 1953. And Oxnard hit 99 degrees Sunday, shattering the daily record of 94 set in 2023.
In Orange County, Anaheim hit 101 degrees Sunday, blowing past the 98-degree record set in 2020.
San Diego hit 100 degrees, toppling a record of 97 set in 1987. The Oceanside Harbor registered 98 on Sunday, toppling the record of 97 set in 1953. And Ramona hit 101, just past the record of 100 set in 1987.
“It’s going to be pretty darn warm,” UC Agriculture and Natural Resources climate scientist Daniel Swain said of this week during a recent briefing on his Weather West channel.
Temperatures between 15 and 22 degrees above normal are expected to persist through Thursday. Highs along the coasts and valleys will be in the 90s up to the low 100s in the coming days. Even the beaches will provide little relief, with temperatures in the upper 80s.
The ocean is expected to bring its own dangers beginning Tuesday with elevated morning and evening tides and elevated surf as a result of Hurricane Rachel, located several hundred miles off the coast of Baja California with sustained winds of up to 85 mph.
The weather service is warning of dangerous rip currents and elevated surf of 3 to 6 feet on Catalina and Santa Barbara Islands as well as at Los Angeles and Ventura County beaches. The most susceptible areas will be Long Beach and the Avalon Harbor on Tuesday and Wednesday and then Malibu through Ventura County from Wednesday through Friday.
“Moderate flooding of sea water is a possibility over some vulnerable low-lying coastal areas, especially around the morning and evening high tides, including over beach parking lots, bike paths, and harbor walkways. Moderate beach erosion is possible to likely,” according to the weather service.
And those looking for relief won’t find it overnight.
It’ll still be warm after dark too, forecasters say, with the mercury dipping only into the upper 60s to mid-70s across much of the region. The weather service in Oxnard and San Diego issued extreme heat warnings through 8 p.m. Thursday, cautioning of the risk of heat-related illnesses.
Schoenfeld said a lack of overnight recovery and days of hot weather can “really build and stress the body over time, especially for the elderly and other vulnerable folks like the very young.”
The Los Angeles Department of Public Health is urging residents to hydrate, avoid going outside during the hottest hours of the day, use an umbrella and wear lightweight clothing if you must go out — and take frequent breaks in air conditioned spaces. The county has dozens of cooling centers open.
The heat is expected to relent a bit by the weekend with temperatures in the mid-80s and even a chance of light showers Sunday as Hurricane Rachel continues its path across the Pacific Ocean.
But Swain, the climate scientist, said models suggest that temperatures won’t decline that much as October continues.
“This is not a cool autumn by any means,” he said.

articles.title_orig: The AI boom is making the world’s cheapest smartphones disappear
articles.title_zh: The AI boom is making the world’s cheapest smartphones disappear
articles.content_orig:
The world’s cheapest smartphones are disappearing because AI infrastructure is absorbing the components.
Prices of existing smartphone models have risen by about 15% globally this year , while newly launched models are roughly 25% more expensive than last year. A global memory chip shortage, driven by demand from AI data centers, is pushing up the cost of making smartphones.
Chinese smartphone makers — which have championed affordable, feature-rich devices and account for approximately 60% of all smartphones shipped globally — have “drastically reduced” their entry-level projects this year as memory-chip costs have risen, Ivan Lam, senior analyst at research firm Counterpoint, told Rest of World . They are instead prioritizing more profitable premium devices.
The smartphone price increases vary sharply by region: They have risen by 21% in India, 19% across Asia-Pacific, and 18% in the Middle East and Africa. In the U.S., they have gone up by just 5%.
The shift could affect more than consumers looking for cheaper phones. For people who have yet to buy their first smartphone, higher prices could make it harder to get online at all — potentially widening the digital divide. The consequences will also reach the U.S. as more essential services move online and the global supply chain for smartphones becomes more expensive.
GSMA, the global mobile industry association, had earlier said nearly 800 million more people will use mobile internet by 2030. But it is concerned that rising smartphone costs would affect this projection and widen the gap of digital inequality, Claire Sibthorpe, head of digital inclusion at the group’s nonprofit foundation, told Rest of World .
“We live in an increasingly digital world, and the proliferation of technologies such as AI is creating greater digital divides and inequities,” Sibthorpe said. “Stakeholders are increasingly using AI to provide access to important services, but people won’t be able to benefit without access to an internet-enabled phone and the internet.”
In 2025, more than one in four smartphones shipped globally cost less than $150 . That market is now shrinking.
Chinese phonemakers including Xiaomi i Xiaomi Xiaomi is a Chinese consumer electronics company that leads the country in smartphone manufacturing and sales. READ MORE , Oppo, Vivo, and Huawei i Huawei Huawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions. READ MORE have built their businesses around offering affordable phones with increasingly sophisticated features. But the economics of that strategy are changing.
What used to be below $150 may become below $250, or even $300.” Ivan Lam, senior analyst, Counterpoint
Chinese companies “would rather reduce investment in products below $150 or $200 and put more resources into higher-margin phones, branding, user experience, and AI,” said Lam.
In India, Xiaomi raised the price of a 128GB Redmi 15C from 12,499 rupees ($140) at launch last December to 16,999 rupees ($190) in June, a 36% increase. In Southeast Asia, Oppo’s sub-$100 phone shipments plunged 96%, and Vivo moved its main entry-level model above $100 in most markets, according to research firm Omdia . In Africa, where 81% of smartphones shipped last year cost less than $200, shipments of sub-$100 phones fell 34% year over year in the second quarter of 2026.
“What used to be below $150 may become below $250, or even $300,” Lam said, adding that he does not expect costs to return to their pre-2025 levels.
The memory-chip shortage is unlikely to ease soon, Ramon Llamas, research director in mobile devices at market research and advisory firm IDC, told Rest of World.
“ There are three primary manufacturers of memory, and in late 2025, all of them pivoted the vast majority of their supply towards AI centers instead of consumer electronics,” Llamas said. “That left many companies scrambling for inventory. … Scarcity of memory has driven up prices for memory, and those price increases have been passed on to the consumer.”
Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology make up more than 90% of the global memory chip market. These companies have entered several partnerships with U.S. AI giants in recent years.
S&P Global has estimated that the capital expenditure of U.S. hyperscalers — Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, and SpaceX — will exceed $1.3 trillion in 2027 , up from a projected $870 billion in 2026 and $470 billion in 2025.
Shipments of sub-$100 smartphones are already falling sharply. The 173 million sub-$100 smartphones shipped globally last year are disappearing, with shipments falling almost 60% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, according to IDC.
For the world’s poorest consumers, the problem is not simply that smartphones are getting more expensive. It’s that the cheapest phones are disappearing.
The price of a smartphone remains a major barrier for lower-income groups to get online, according to GSMA’s September report. An entry-level device costs the poorest 20% the equivalent of 44% of their monthly income, and 76% for people in sub-Saharan Africa.
When smartphones remain available but become unaffordable, consumers make difficult sacrifices to keep themselves online.” Claire Sibthorpe, head of digital inclusion at GSMA’s foundation
For many lower-income consumers, gains in income are unlikely to keep pace with the sudden rise in handset prices.
“When smartphones remain available but become unaffordable, consumers make difficult sacrifices to keep themselves online. They might delay upgrading, borrow or share their devices, remain on older feature phones, or go offline when they are unable to replace a device that is no longer working or stolen. Often, it means they won’t have an internet-enabled device at all,” Sibthorpe said.

For much of his life, Zain Javaid, 19, wanted to be a quant who uses math and data to guide his investment decisions. And for a while, he was one. But he got bored. Then, in 2022, ChatGPT was released, and he told TechCrunch, “I felt fundamentally excited in a way that I never had been before.”
He became interested in personal AI, and that interest led him to start Ghost, which announced Monday that it has emerged from stealth after a year of building, along with an $11 million seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz. Other investors in the round include Abstract, Audacious Ventures, SV Angel, and Nova. His founding team includes Nicholas Chua, 19, Yifei Chen, 24, and Gautam Sharda, 23.
Ghost’s first product is Core, a personal computer designed specifically for AI agents that can take actions on a person’s behalf. According to Javaid, the idea is to centralize a person’s data, from what’s on their desktop to apps to smart home devices, into one piece of hardware designed to continuously run AI agents that can act as an assistant, perform tasks, and understand a person’s life. “You can run models on existing hardware, but it’s a terrible experience on many levels,” said Javaid, who is also Core’s CEO.
Core includes an Nvidia RTX Pro 4000 SFF Blackwell GPU (a type of chip commonly used to run AI models), said Javaid, adding that the GPU is bundled into the device’s price, so customers don’t need to buy one separately. He said it also has its own software layer, browser, and filing system and can continuously process information and tasks without constant prompting. Core costs $3,499. Preorders for the first batch open Monday, and shipping is scheduled for the last week of October.
Javaid described Core as a “brain in a box” without a screen, which users access through a phone or app. Voice mode is also available, but users must speak into the Core app rather than the box itself. Core comes with three models preinstalled: Qwen-3.8-Next, Qwen-3.8-27B, and Gemma-4-31B.
Javaid said users can also install other models from Hugging Face, where developers share AI models, or load their own trained models. Asked how Core differs from a Mac Mini, Apple’s small desktop computer that some people set up to run AI tools, Javaid said Core’s hardware and software were built specifically for running AI agents, with models already installed, while the Mac Mini is a general-purpose computer that can be configured for AI.
“As new models or improvements to existing models come out, we can push out over-the-air updates, similar to how Tesla works,” Javaid said of Core, adding that if a new generation of models comes out, the company asks users whether they want to switch. “Users can also turn on auto-updates so they’re always running the latest generation of a given model.”
The team currently builds the units at its San Francisco facility. Javaid said the goal is to sell a fully functioning computer that doesn’t require complex setup or configuration. He said the models and personal memory run locally, and that all personal information is encrypted so that no cloud provider or third party, including Ghost, can meaningfully access it. He also said users can control how much autonomy they give their Core agents, and that the device is programmed to keep working if Ghost shuts down.
“All of the source code, logic, and model weights live on the device, not the services,” he said. “We build this device to not be dependent on having an outside entity maintaining the service.”
He said the team is also building a firewall to limit how the agent can use its credentials, such as logins and passwords. The firewall “monitors every outgoing network request on the computer and if it sees the agent performing a sanctioned action or exfiltrating data it shouldn’t, it rejects the request and flags it for user review.”
“The user owns all of it,” he said of the device, memory, and data. “Once you buy the hardware, everything is stored, run, and processed on the device.”
He said he is not too worried about the competition, including from established tech companies. “People sometimes give incumbents credit for having already built the product because they have the ingredients,” he said. He credited Apple with good hardware and disruption, but said much of what Core is aiming to tackle is software: “The model reasons over your life, how it remembers, how it takes action, how it knows when to reach out,” he continued.
Javaid offered an example of how Core is meant to work: “Core proactively sends you a notification that you might be getting sick because it sees your resting heart rate is elevated, sees from computer history that you were up late working on a project, and has seasonal context that it is flu season in San Francisco.”
The company’s main focus is building a product people love, he said. “If we can’t do that, Apple isn’t the reason we failed,” he said.

articles.title_orig: DP World plots US port comeback with Corpus Christi container terminal
articles.title_zh: DP World plots US port comeback with Corpus Christi container terminal
articles.content_orig:
Global terminal operator DP World has taken another step toward returning to U.S. port operations two decades after a proposed takeover of terminals at several major American ports raised concerns over national security.
The Port of Corpus Christi, Texas, has signed a lease option agreement with Dubai-based DP World to develop a container terminal capable of eventually handling about 1 million twenty-foot equivalent units annually, according to a port official.
“We’ve signed a lease option agreement with DP World for a development … of a container terminal in the Port,” Jeffrey Pollack, chief strategy and sustainability officer for the Port of Corpus Christi Authority, told the American Journal of Transportation during the American Association of Port Authorities annual convention in New Orleans on Sept. 29.
Corpus Christi currently is not a container port, and Pollack said adding container operations would significantly diversify a cargo base heavily centered on energy.
Pollack said officials envision a relatively modest container operation by the standards of the largest U.S. gateways, with capacity ultimately topping out around 1 million TEUs annually.
The agreement represents a significant potential return to U.S. marine terminal operations for DP World.
The company, which is owned by the government of Dubai in the United Arab Emirates, became the center of a major political controversy in 2006 after its acquisition of British terminal operator P&O would have transferred P&O’s terminal leases and operations at several major U.S. ports to DP World.
The deal triggered bipartisan opposition in Congress over national security concerns and ultimately led DP World to divest P&O’s U.S. port operations, according to the U.S. Senate Commerce Committee’s Feb. 28, 2006 hearing, “Security of Terminal Operations at U.S. Ports.”
DP World ultimately announced in March 2006 that it would divest P&O’s U.S. operations after lawmakers moved to block the transaction. The controversy came despite the George W. Bush administration’s support for the transaction and its position that port security would remain under the responsibility of U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the Coast Guard.
The Corpus Christi project would mark DP World’s first U.S. container terminal development since that episode and its first container terminal development on the U.S. Gulf Coast.
DP World is one of the world’s largest terminal operators, handling roughly 10% of global container traffic through more than 60 ports and terminals.
DP World and the Port of Corpus Christi first announced in June that they had entered exclusive negotiations for a long-term lease. Under the proposed development, DP World would design, build and operate the terminal.
At the time, the parties said negotiations would focus on terminal design, capacity planning and the project’s investment structure.
The project could significantly alter Corpus Christi’s position in Gulf Coast freight markets.
The port is one of the nation’s largest gateways by total tonnage but has historically focused on crude oil, liquefied natural gas, refined petroleum products, agricultural commodities and industrial cargo rather than containers.
Corpus Christi also recently acquired about 2,000 acres roughly 8 to 10 miles south of its Inner Harbor that port officials envision as an inland port supporting the proposed container terminal.
Pollack said the property can connect with all three Class I railroads serving the port and multiple interstate highway systems, potentially attracting manufacturing, warehousing and other import-export operations.
The container push comes as Corpus Christi continues posting record overall cargo volumes. Customers moved 110.3 million tons through the Corpus Christi Ship Channel during the first half of 2026, up 7.7% from the previous first-half record of 102.4 million tons set a year earlier.
Why it matters: The project at the Port of Corpus Christi, Texas, would bring DP World back into U.S. container terminal operations two decades after national security concerns in Congress derailed its acquisition of terminal operations at several major American ports.

articles.title_orig: How the Nike x ‘One Piece’ Collaboration Joined the Lore-Filled World — NIKE, Inc.
articles.title_zh: How the Nike x ‘One Piece’ Collaboration Joined the Lore-Filled World — NIKE, Inc.
articles.content_orig:
Since it initially published in 1997, the Japanese manga series ONE PIECE has surpassed 600 million copies in its circulation, on par with the biggest superhero comics and most popular wizarding-world books. To call creator Eiichiro Oda’s series a cultural behemoth would be like calling ONE PIECE ’s legendary “Blue Sea” a mere body of water — technically true, but wildly short of it.
Dr. B’s Research Lab at Nike’s Harajuku pop-up, recasting Bill Bowerman as a scientist studying the Devil Fruit–inspired Air Max Plus collabs. Here, the three models hang suspended like specimens.
You can call it manifest destiny that the world’s most popular manga and the world’s largest sports company would join forces at some point . But for Nike to honor the legacy of a pop culture landmark so robust and influential that fans literally name their children after characters, it couldn’t just be a simple merch collaboration. Instead, Nike answered with three Air Max Plus silhouettes, each inspired by a Devil Fruit (from ONE PIECE lore), apparel stitched with references only the faithful will catch, and a globe-trotting rollout meant to be explored like the story it came from. With a mythology this deep and only one shot to engage with the canon, Nike Virtual Studios’ .SWOOSH team knew it had to come correct.
“When a brand collabs with ‘ONE PIECE,’ they are creating something new for the community; they are adding to the incredibly rich lore of the story.”
“When a brand collabs with ONE PIECE , they are creating something new for the community; they are adding to the incredibly rich lore of the story,” says Ashwin Shinde, .SWOOSH's Senior Manager, Energy Gaming Product Merch on Nike’s ONE PIECE Collection. “So, we lean on the thing that’s always going to set us apart from other brands. What is a story that only Nike could tell?”
For .SWOOSH, the answer started with a conceptual parallel. “We took the spirit of Nike and its desire to push people beyond their human potential and combined it with the Devil Fruits, which literally give people the ability to go beyond human potential and essentially have superpowers,” says Bryce Wong, Senior Manager, Gaming Footwear Product Design.
Bridging the two brand universes, the team landed on a single idea: “If Devil Fruits existed in our world, they would be Nikes.” From there, the task became choosing the right shoe to bring it to life. Wong proposed the Air Max Plus, an iconic model whose expressive cage and dimensional upper made it, in the words of Senior Designer Yuchung Chen, “a perfect design to blend with the whimsical world of ONE PIECE .”
Translating a superpower-inducing fruit into the shoe meant reworking every surface. “Each Devil Fruit design posed its own challenge of maintaining the motion and directionality of the original shoe’s cage design while keeping it light and open,” says Chen, who wrapped the fruit pattern across the mudguard, cage and shank. Each upper got its own finish: gummy and rubber-like for Gum Gum, a velvety peach-fuzz for Ope Ope, and an on-fire sunset for Mera Mera that nods to the OG Air Max Plus.
The deepest cut is on the medial shank: a contrasting color bites a chunk clean out, a reference to the panel where rubber-limbed hero Monkey D. Luffy accidentally eats the Gum Gum fruit — or, as Chen noted in a wink for the heads, it has another, real name — thinking of it as dessert.
“We took the spirit of Nike and its desire to push people beyond their human potential and combined it with the Devil
Fruits, which literally give people the ability to go beyond human potential. If Devil Fruits existed
in our world, they would be Nikes.”
The apparel scaled the same logic up: mythical fruit into tangible object, rendered on fabric. “Following that same approach, the patterns, colors and textures of the Devil Fruits that inspired the footwear are enlarged and abstracted into layered graphics,” explains Lead, Global Brand Digital Designer, Sarah Kim. This makes each piece a “wearable abstraction of the shoes and, by extension, the fruits themselves.”
She built the graphic tees around Laboon — the whale character who waits years for the promised return of his old friends, making a promise with Luffy  — because of the way his endurance speaks to both sides of the collab at once. “We wanted the choices to ultimately communicate the shared ethos of a Nike athlete and a shonen manga hero: resilience, perseverance and the ability to keep going.”
The building takeover in Shanghai, including a Straw Hats’ Jolly Roger reworked with a Swoosh for crossbones, beside a flaming “WANT ’EM” ad wrapping the space.
The team also used canonical deep cuts to inject the collaboration with inside jokes that will make loyalists salivate. This includes a vest that nods to one of the manga’s core rules, that Devil Fruit consumers trade their ability to swim for their powers. “The vest was an addition that emerged as a meta and cheeky way to play into the lore as we got deeper into development and more immersed in the ONE PIECE universe,” says Kim.
Inside Dr. B’s Research Lab, including the “hated by the sea” vest.
The same investment into authenticity even shaped the release’s packaging. Open the shoebox and your reflection stares back from a “Wanted” poster printed inside, casting buyers as pirates with bounties on their heads, like so many of the ONE PIECE heroes. “The idea behind the mirror was to make the person opening the box part of the story,” says Global Brand Experience Designer Heena Chung. “Your reflection completes the poster and, for a second, you become part of the ONE PIECE world.” She designed the packaging as a “treasure chest” with a staged reveal, down to a reward for completists: line up all three boxes and the Devil Fruit graphics connect into a single panoramic artwork.
The unboxing was intentionally designed to unfold in stages, like a treasure chest built to reveal itself over time. Printed tissue gives way to a trading card; the shoes wait beneath as the prize.
Between the lid and the shoes, printed tissue paper hides its own ONE PIECE iconography. “There’s a deliberate progression to the reveal,” says Chung. “The exterior establishes the collaboration, the tissue introduces another layer of the world, and the mirror creates the final interaction by placing you directly inside the Wanted poster.”
The IYKYK references are dense and intentional, but they aren’t the raison d'être. “The bigger goal was to capture the feeling of ONE PIECE rather than simply collect Easter eggs,” says Chung. “The box becomes part of the collaboration itself — something worth keeping and exploring rather than just a container for the product.”
“The bigger goal was to capture the feeling of ‘ONE PIECE’ rather than simply collect Easter eggs.”
A collection this considered could have simply dropped, no problem. Instead, the deep bench of the global .SWOOSH team took it off the shelf and into the wild by staging physical activations across nearly two dozen cities worldwide, turning the release into something fans can travel to and track down. The blueprint came straight from the source. ”“Creatively, the table was already set by Oda’s story of the ONE PIECE protagonist and his crew, known as the Straw Hats, traveling the world and searching for treasure,” says Wong. “We wanted to parallel that with the world of sneaker collecting, giving people a reason to find their crew, discover, and experience something different along the way.”
Dr. B’s mobile lab, parked in Harajuku and rigged out. Nike’s answer to Dr. Vegapunk, the ‘ONE PIECE’ scientist who studies the Devil Fruits.
That hunt materialized city by city. In the Harajuku district of Tokyo, a Nike-branded Poneglyph — one of the manga’s ancient, indestructible tablets inscribed in a lost language — appeared on Cat Street, teasing the release with no explanation unless you’re fluent in the saga. Below the Nike store there, the team built out Dr. B’s Research Lab, a nod to Dr. Vegap

articles.title_orig: New UNESCO data: For every two teachers, the world needs one more
articles.title_zh: New UNESCO data: For every two teachers, the world needs one more
articles.content_orig:
A new fact sheet released by the UNESCO Institute for Statistics and the International Task Force on Teachers for Education 2030 examines the status of teachers, including how teachers are valued, supported and paid, 60 years after the adoption of the landmark 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers .
The fact sheet was released to mark World Teachers’ Day 2026 , bringing together ministers, teachers and education experts at UNESCO Headquarters in Paris to discuss how to strengthen the profession. Co-convened by UNESCO, the International Labour Organization, UNICEF and Education International, the celebration took place under the theme “Standing with teachers: 60 years of protecting the profession, advancing its status and shaping our futures”.
Every learner deserves a teacher who is well prepared, well supported and empowered to thrive in the profession. Realizing this right depends on how societies value teachers and the teaching profession. In fact, the value we place on teachers reflects the value we place on future generation.
How teachers are seen by society shapes whether they stay in their jobs. In 75% of the countries taking part in the OECD's TALIS 2024 survey , fewer than 40% of teachers felt that their profession was valued. Those who felt valued were over 10% less likely to think about leaving within five years.
The stakes are high: 58% of the teachers the world needs by 2030 will be hired not to expand the workforce, but to replace those who leave the profession. The fact sheet shows where the losses are greatest: attrition rates are 7.2% in pre-primary education, 5.4% in secondary and 4.7% in primary.
The new data also reveals that pre-primary and primary teachers earn slightly less than other professionals with similar qualifications. Overall, in two out of five of the 68 countries analyzed, teacher salaries remain below those of similarly qualified professionals across all education levels.
Teaching also comes with a heavy workload.  Teachers spend an average of 19 hours in the classroom per week, but work around 60 hours in total, much of it includes unpaid preparation, marking and administrative tasks. In primary schools, the global pupil-trained teacher ratio stands at 28 to 1, the highest of any level.
The fact sheet offers practical recommendations for governments and partners. These include giving teachers a seat at the table when policy is made, setting professional standards and career paths, offering competitive salaries and targeted incentives for hard-to-staff schools, making schools safer and more supportive, and cutting back unnecessary workload.
UNESCO works with countries to increase the supply of qualified, motivated teachers by improving policies relating to them and supporting quality training which meets learners’ needs. Special focus is placed on Africa, inclusion, gender sensitivity and digital technologies.
UNESCO and the ILO have also launched a joint revision of the 1966 Recommendation , guided by an Independent Expert Group through mid-2027.
As the work moves forward, the evidence is clear: attractive, respected and supported teaching professions are the foundation of quality education for every learner.

articles.title_orig: Dennis Hastert, former US speaker from Illinois convicted in Yorkville High School hush money case, dies at Plano home
articles.title_zh: Dennis Hastert, former US speaker from Illinois convicted in Yorkville High School hush money case, dies at Plano home
articles.content_orig:
Judge called Hastert a 'serial child molester' during sentencing in Yorkville High School hush money case
CHICAGO (WLS) -- An Illinois politician who rose from local office to become speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives - and later fell into disgrace - has died. Dennis Hastert died Saturday at his home in Plano while in hospice care. He was 84.
Hastert's oncetowering political legacy was irreversibly damaged after he admitted, years after leaving Congress, to sexually abusing boys he coached while working as a wrestling coach at Yorkville High School.
Hastert, a former teacher from Kendall County, climbed rapidly through Illinois politics and onto the national stage.
He later reflected on his unlikely rise, saying, "I never envisioned that this former teacher and wrestling coach from Kendall County, Illinois would have the opportunity to lead the United States House of Representatives."
Hastert served as speaker from 1999 to 2007, becoming the longestserving Republican to hold the position. Pat Brady, a former Illinois GOP chairman, said Hastert was "very effective as a legislator," noting the socalled Hastert rule requiring enough Republican support before bringing a bill forward.
"Which was what Republicans wanted," Brady said.
Hastert retired after Democrats won control of the House, but his reputation soon unraveled. Federal prosecutors said that in 2010 he began meeting secretly with someone identified only as Individual A. In a 2015 plea agreement, Hastert admitted he had agreed to "provide Individual A $3,500,000 in order to compensate for and keep confidential his prior misconduct against Individual A."
A lawsuit later alleged the payments were hush money tied to sexual abuse during a high school wrestling trip. More victims came forward, including former Yorkville wrestler Scott Cross, who said, "Dennis Hastert was a monster yet he was protected by outdated laws."
Cross testified publicly about the harm he said Hastert inflicted, stating, "Hastert inflicted unbelievable pain on the lives of the youth he was entrusted to care for."
Hastert was ultimately sentenced to federal prison, serving 13 months on banking fraud charges connected to the payments. Brady said the downfall was stark: "He went to the highest level of politics and then came down in flames," noting that the sentencing judge described Hastert as "a serial child molester."
No one answered the door at Hastert's home Monday.

articles.title_orig: What if the world hadn't built wind and solar?
articles.title_zh: What if the world hadn't built wind and solar?
articles.content_orig:
Twenty years ago, wind, solar and other non-hydro renewables were close to a rounding error. In 2005 they supplied a mere 2.0% of the world’s electricity generation. By 2015 that had risen to 6.8%, and by 2025 it was up to 19.8%. According to the IEA Electricity 2026 outlook, non-hydro renewables will supply around 21.8% of global electricity in 2026, edging past natural gas (21.6%) to become the second-largest source of power after coal. 1
That is a remarkable pace of growth from an industry that barely existed two decades ago. But not everyone is impressed; many commenters on social media have responded to these figures by pointing out that despite the growth of renewables, fossil fuel generation continues to grow as well. They aren’t wrong; global coal generation set a record in 2024. Gas generation reached a new high in 2025.
Their point is that clean energy isn’t replacing fossil fuels at all. It’s simply being piled on top of them to feed an ever-growing appetite for electricity, making this an “energy addition” rather than an energy transition. Global fossil electricity generation around 50% higher today than it was in 2005. Coal generation rose by 3,300 TWh and gas by 3,200 TWh. The world burns more coal for power now than it did when wind and solar started taking off.
This argument has been made in the past both by skeptics of growth and by energy systems modelers. The historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz argues in More and More and More (2024) that “far from the industrial era passing through a series of transformations, each new phase has in practice remained almost wholly entangled with the previous one.” Coal mining created a huge new demand for timber for pit props, while the oil age ran on steel made with coal. Vaclav Smil has made the same point about today’s clean energy boom more bluntly: ”We use more fossil fuels today than at any time in history… Renewables are not replacing fossil fuels; are joining them.”
The problem with the “addition” argument is that it compares the world today with the world in 2005, rather than with the world as it would have been without clean energy. Electricity demand has not grown because wind turbines and solar panels were built. It has grown because of what the IEA describes as “rising consumption from industry, electric vehicles, air conditioning and data centers”. Demand growth is located overwhelmingly in emerging and developing economies, which accounted for about 80% of global demand growth in 2025 and an average of 95% over the past decade.
Global electricity demand rose by 75% (13,600 TWh) between 2005 and 2025. That demand had to be met by something. Wind and solar supplied 5,400 TWh of new demand, hydro 1,500 TWh, bioenergy and other renewables 530 TWh, nuclear 85 TWh, and fossil fuels the remaining 6,100 TWh. But over the past decade the balance has shifted sharply toward clean energy. Since 2015, wind and solar supplied 57% of demand growth, compared with 29% for fossil fuels. And in 2025, according to Ember’s Global Electricity Review 2026 , “wind and solar grew by 841 TWh, meeting 99% of global electricity demand growth”.
A 2024 study by Brantley Liddle found that “intermittent renewables (solar and wind) have unitary displacement effect.” In other words, each unit of wind and solar power displaced about one unit of coal and oil generation. Fossil generation has kept rising in many years because demand has grown faster than clean energy could be added. That is very different from clean energy failing to displace anything.
And electricity demand will continue to rapidly grow, particularly if we succeed in reducing global emissions by electrifying sectors of the economy that currently burn fossil fuels. Most scenarios where we reach net zero emissions involve a doubling or tripling of electricity generation.
So if we want to assess the real world emissions impact of wind and solar buildout over the past 20 years, the right question to ask is not “did fossil use go down?” but rather “how much higher would it have been?”
To answer this, I built a counterfactual for the global power sector in which wind and solar (and geothermal, which is less than 2% of the total) stopped growing in 2005. In every separate country, their generation is held at 2005 levels, while electricity demand, nuclear, hydro and bioenergy follow their real-world paths. 2 The missing clean generation has to come from somewhere, and in this counterfactual it comes from fossil fuels.
The key choice is which fossil fuels are used to fill in the gap. A wind farm in China or India displaces coal, while one in Texas or the UK mostly displaces gas. So rather than assuming a single global fossil mix, the analysis fills each country’s gap with that country’s own coal, gas and oil mix in each year, using data for about 200 countries from Ember . This keeps real-world coal-to-gas switching like what occurred during the US shale gas boom in place, rather than crediting it to renewables. 3
Without wind and solar growth since 2005, global power-sector CO2 emissions in 2025 would have been 28% higher, at 16.9 billion tonnes rather than 13.2 billion. This adds up to 3.7 billion tonnes avoided in 2025, which is about three-quarters of the total CO2 US emissions that year (or roughly 1.5x EU emissions).
Between 2006 and 2025, wind and solar avoided about 23 billion tonnes of CO2. The biggest assumption I’ve made is what fossil fuel fills in the gap: if every missing kilowatt-hour had come from gas, avoided emissions would be 15 billion tonnes, while if it was all coal it would have been 30 billion.
This lines up almost exactly with Ember’s own estimate. Using a simpler method (and a 2000 baseline rather than 2005 baseline), Ember’s Global Electricity Review 2026 found that “had wind and solar not grown since 2000, fossil generation would have been 30% higher in 2025, and emissions 28% higher.”
While its true that global electricity emissions have yet to clearly peak, it may well be imminent; emissions went down in 2025 and may be on track to decline in 2026 as well, though rapid increases in demand from vehicle electrification and data centers have made this a bit more challenging. 4 But there are many countries in which electricity emissions have already peaked and declined substantially, and where clean energy has played a key role in those declines.
Globally, clean energy has not yet led to fossil fuel use peaking in the electricity sector. In 2025, fossil generation was essentially flat (down ~0.3%). But that global total hides a lot of country-level variability. In many wealthier economies, where demand has grown more slowly, clean energy has driven real emissions reductions (even when accounting for the outsourcing of some industrial production).
Between 2005 and 2025, power-sector CO2 emissions fell by 75% in the UK, 55% in the European Union and 37% in the United States.
The reasons why differ from place to place:
In the EU, wind and solar account for about 85% of the decline (512 of 601 million tonnes), even though falling nuclear output pushed emissions up by about 100 million tonnes.
In the UK, the decline had three main drivers: wind and solar (56 million tonnes), lower domestic generation (58 million tonnes, partly because the UK now imports more power), and the near-elimination of coal, which went from 45% of UK fossil generation to effectively zero (36 million tonnes).
In the US, switching from coal to cheaper natural gas cut emissions by 682 million tonnes, slightly more than wind and solar (606 million tonnes), while a 12% rise in electricity use added 352 million tonnes. Coal’s share of US fossil generation fell from 69% to 29%.
Without wind and solar growth, EU power emissions would have fallen by only about 16% since 2005 rather than 55%, US emissions by about 17% rather than 37%, and UK emissions by about 53% rather than 75%. In these regions clean energy has not just met new demand, its actually pushed fossil generation d

U.S. News & World Report and The Princeton Review have ranked the University of Lynchburg among the nation’s best colleges and universities.
In its 2027 edition of “Best Colleges,” U.S. News ranked Lynchburg 332nd among National Universities and 154th in the Top Private Schools category. Lynchburg’s nursing program ranked 557th, and the University ranked 329th in Top Performers on Social Mobility, which recognizes schools that “performed best in … Pell Grant graduation rates and Pell Grant graduation rate performance.”
Lynchburg also is listed in “The Best 392 Colleges: 2027 Edition,” published by The Princeton Review. Lynchburg also was ranked among The Princeton Review’s “Best Mid-Atlantic” colleges and universities.
“These recognitions demonstrate the strength of the University of Lynchburg community,” said Dr. Sally Selden, the University’s president. “We offer an education grounded in academic excellence, personal connection, and student engagement.
“Our students thrive because they are supported by faculty and staff who are deeply committed to their success, both in and out of the classroom. I’m proud of the work happening across our campus and grateful that our student experience is being recognized nationally.”
According to U.S. News, its “Best Colleges” are “ranked according to their performance across widely accepted indicators of excellence.” You can read more about the methodology U.S. News uses to compile its rankings here .
The Princeton Review stated that its 2027 list “brings together survey results from over 172,000 students across the country to find out what they love the most about these schools in everything from financial aid and career services to sustainability and quality of life.”
Those surveyed about the University of Lynchburg described its students as “friendly and willing to work together and help each other out” and said the University was “beginning to have more cultural diversity.” Its reputation for “Southern hospitality” was also noted.
One student put it this way: “Everyone is very helping. If someone is not able to help you with a homework question or a project, then they will find you someone who can. It does feel like one giant family here.”

articles.title_zh: Ebola outbreak shows that the world is not ready for the next pandemic
articles.content_orig:
As Ebola continues to spread in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, the burning question at recent UN pandemic preparedness meetings at the UN General Assembly was: Is the world willing and able to pay for readiness?
When the Marburg virus hit Rwanda in September 2024, the country’s No. 1 goal was stopping community transmission. Marburg, in the same family as the Ebola virus, is second among the top-four deadliest viruses in the world. More than 80 per cent of people who contract the disease die.
The country tracked the source of the zoonotic disease, and using genomic sequencing, sequenced the virus. They discovered that the outbreak was closely related to a sequence that happened in an outbreak of Marburg in Uganda in 2014.
Rwanda mounted an ambitious response by beginning contact tracing, mass testing and surveillance. Ultimately, 9.6 million people were screened by about 54,000 community health workers.
From the diagnosis of the first case of Marburg to the deployment of the first shot of the experimental Sabin Vaccine Institute inoculation was 10 days. The case fatality rate for the outbreak stayed at 22 per cent, the lowest ever recorded for the virus.
Two years on, across the border from Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), has entered Day 139 of its fight against a new strain of an Ebola outbreak, called Bundibugyo. Approximately 3,700 people have died since the outbreak was declared in mid-May 2026. The first encouraging signs of progress to fight it may be emerging.
Rwanda’s response to the Marburg outbreak, hailed the world over, was possible because the country had spent years preparing for such an epidemic. But the DRC is trying to build responses in altogether different conditions: It is coping with a humanitarian crisis amid a war.
So the burning question that dominated the UN’s pandemic preparedness meetings at the General Assembly high-level session last week was: Is the world willing and able to pay for readiness now?
According to the WHO, from 31 August to 20 September, the cases of Ebola in the DRC declined by approximately 26 per cent at the epicenter, Ituri Province. However, in the same period, North Kivu Province, near Ituri, recorded a 73 per cent increase, evidence that the outbreak was evolving across the numerous affected areas.
“Each of the seven affected provinces has its own transmission pattern. One of our greatest concerns is that too many people are still dying before reaching treatment,” said Dr. Marie Roseline Belizaire, the regional emergency director for WHO Africa. She was speaking by Zoom at a recent UN briefing on the Ebola outbreak in eastern DRC and emergency preparedness ahead of El Niño and other health emergencies in the region.
“Every death in the community also increases the risk of further transmission among family members, caregivers, and others involved in burial practices, and although adults account for most confirmed cases,” Dr. Belizaire added. “Children are especially vulnerable.”
On the ground in the DRC, she said that all response teams are working closely with communities to identify suspected cases quickly and to address the misinformation that is keeping people from seeking appropriate care. The bigger emphasis has been moving the response away from major urban centers into rural areas, where the most-worrying epidemiologic trends are occurring.
“The problem is multifaceted,” Dr. Catherine Smallwood, a WHO incident manager for the Ebola response in North Kivu, said in the recent UN event. “There is the access one, and there’s also the issue of funding. We need partners. We need time, we need money, we have a plan, and if we really, truly want to be able to stop this epidemic in the next six months, we will need additional resources.”
For both Rwanda and the DRC, the realities of fighting the Bundibugyo strain are vastly distinct. Rwanda’s health minister, Yvan Butera, spoke at an event during the UN high-level week hosted by the Pandemic Fund, which focuses on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response in low- and middle-income countries, and the governments of Armenia and Rwanda. The forum spotlighted how countries are investing their own resources to close critical preparedness gaps.
Butera said that building a readiness-response plan cannot be done in the middle of a war and humanitarian disaster. The DRC’s effort to control the Ebola outbreak is still lacking an approved vaccine. Provisions of other essential health services are also being carried out under sometimes deadly circumstances.
The services include maternal health, routine immunizations, treatments of malaria and other baseline conditions resulting from widespread displacement of civilians. The decades-long conflict in the eastern DRC involves the M23 militia from Rwanda fighting Congolese troops in competition for the area’s mineral wealth. The violence has made the Ebola outbreak hard to contain.
As of 30 September 2026, data from the Congolese authorities confirmed a total of 3,901 deaths out of 8,067 confirmed cases in the DRC from the outbreak. It has surpassed previous records to become the largest Ebola outbreak in the history of the DRC, but it has not spread to Rwanda. In May 2026, it spread into neighboring Uganda through infected cross-border travelers, but its government halted transmission and was officially declared virus-free by the WHO in August 2026.
Six years ago, the Covid-19 pandemic devastated global health systems, and many countries have yet to fully recover. Mathematical modeling by the Center for Global Development , a nongovernmental organization focused on reducing poverty, suggests that the likelihood of another pandemic of the same scale as Covid within the next 25 years will hit nearly 70 percent. Many global health experts believe the odds are climbing closer to a full certainty.
But the world moves on too quickly, said Wessam Mankoula, the acting head of Emergency Preparedness and Response Division for Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or Africa CDC.
“SARS is over and we forgot, Covid-19 came, we’ve forgotten the devastation,” Mankoula said in a panel on building resilience during last week’s UN General Assembly session. “We need to invest more to build resilient systems now. And to ensure sustainability of our efforts, in the DRC and everywhere else we have to first fight our serious case of pandemic Alzheimer’s.”
Mankoula’s work involves generating resources for the Pandemic Fund to remedy the Ebola outbreak in the DRC. His team is aiming for a fast turnaround of financial pledges into disbursement.
“In the first two months of the response in DRC, we had 10 to 20 per cent success moving from pledges to disbursement,” he said. “The impact was that the first response plan for DRC was $240 million and the second response plan was $1.3 billion. So when there is a delay in dispersing resources, the cost of responding to an emergency dramatically increases.”
According to media reports , $2.9 billion has been raised so far, based on Africa CDC numbers.
Success, Mankoula added, is when the CDC’s support is no longer needed because countries got their pandemic readiness done in “peace time.”
The World Bank operates the Pandemic Fund, whose largest contributors are the US, the European Commission, Germany, Italy and Japan.
“The World Bank and the Pandemic Fund’s priorities are clear. Invest early, invest together, and be ready to act,” Paschal Donohoe, the managing director and chief knowledge officer at the World Bank said at the General Assembly event.
“We learned from the pandemic [Covid-19] that countries that depended on others for the tools that they needed to survive paid a price,” he added.

This past Thursday (Oct. 1), four brave souls launched off our planet, headed to an orbiting laboratory where they will spend the next six months living and working.
SpaceX's Crew-13 mission for NASA launched last week, sending four astronauts on a journey from Earth to the International Space Station (ISS). They lifted off on a Crew Dragon capsule atop a Falcon 9 rocket.
The crew consists of NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov. Watkins is commanding the mission, and it is her second time to space. Crew-13 is the first mission for the other three.
Crew-13 was originally supposed to launch on Sept. 12, but an issue with its Crew Dragon delayed things a bit. The mission launched from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, reaching orbit just 10 minutes later and the ISS in less than eight hours . No American spacecraft had ever chased down the orbiting lab in less time.
This photograph shows the moment of launch in striking black and white infrared, which really highlights the intense heat and power coming from the rocket.
This image captures the drama and power of spaceflight. With smoke billowing out from under the rocket's fiery engines, it is incredible to think that in the tiny capsule on the very top of the rocket sit four human beings, strapped in, leaving our planet behind.
Rocket launches are exciting, but there is something especially amazing about sending people to outer space that separates these events from the others.
And, like other crewed missions, these astronauts have a big job ahead of them. They'll work alongside the other astronauts on the ISS on a variety of science experiments and perform maintenance on the station itself.

articles.title_orig: Apple event is reportedly happening next week, per Mark Gurman
articles.title_zh: Apple event is reportedly happening next week, per Mark Gurman
articles.content_orig:
Apple is expected to launch several new products next week on October 13, and per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the product unveilings will happen at “an event.” Here’s what he said.
We’re nearly a month out from the last Apple event, which featured the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, and more.
But it sounds like an October event could be on the way as early as next Tuesday, October 13.
Per Mark Gurman, writing in his Power On newsletter :
Apple is planning to hold an event on Oct. 13 to unveil its long-awaited smart home hub with a screen, the new HomePod mini and an updated Apple TV. All three devices will have Siri AI at the core.
Gurman previously reported that these three products would be launching October 13, but at the time he made no mention of an event.
There’s been plenty of speculation about whether these new Home products would merit an event or not. John Gruber, for example, said there was “No way” that the rumored HomePad would be released via a press release only. He wrote, “if this is coming, it has to be unveiled with a keynote video and some sort of media event with hands-on demos.”
And based on his latest newsletter, Gurman clearly believes that’s what’s happening. “Apple is planning to hold an event on Oct. 13” sounds pretty straightforward.
If an event does happen, we would expect to see press invites go out in the next day or so. Unless, of course, new CEO John Ternus plans to shake up the way does product introductions and bucks prior patterns.
Do you think Apple’s Home devices will be unveiled at a proper October event or via press releases? Let us know in the comments.
